full_text:
Veteran edge rusher Samson Ebukam is one of the players the Falcons may rely on for getting after the opposing quarterback. Dale Zanine / Imagn Images
FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. — In 2025, the Atlanta Falcons set a franchise record with 57 sacks. Twenty-six of those sacks are now gone, and another 12 are in limbo as the team has a serious problem at edge rusher.
The math: Jalon Walker (5.5 sacks) was lost for the season due to a torn ACL last week. Ruke Orhorhoro (3.5) was traded, and Kaden Elliss (3.5), Leonard Floyd (3.5), Ronnie Harrison (2), Kentavius Street (2), Dee Alford (2), Arnold Ebiketie (2), David Onyemata (1) and Sam Roberts (1) left via free agency. James Pearce Jr. (10.5) could face a lengthy suspension from the NFL after his offseason arrest, and Billy Bowman Jr. (1.5) still hasn’t returned to the practice field after last season’s Achilles tear.
So now what? First, the Falcons have to get over the shock of Walker’s loss. Despite having just one year of NFL experience, the University of Georgia product was expected to have an outsized influence on the defense because of his versatility and maturity.
“We all know what he means to the team,” outside linebackers coach John Timu said. “When he comes in, we feel it. Huge loss.”
Walker, the 15th pick in the 2025 draft, had 36 tackles, six quarterback hurries and five tackles for loss on top of his 5.5 sacks while starting nine games last year, and he had taken almost every snap with the starters in training camp practices leading up to his injury.
“That’s the worst part of this game, stuff like that,” offensive tackle Jake Matthews said. “He’s one of the leaders of our defense. He’s a vocal guy. He leads by example. He’s always in the right place. The leadership role he took on at such a young age is really impressive.”
Now the Falcons have to replace not only that leadership but Walker’s production on the field.
“To see Jalon go down was disappointing and frustrating for him, but I know what he’s made of. He will bounce back,” coach Kevin Stefanski said. “In the interim, like any injury or player being unavailable, we just have to make sure we have a plan defensively to move guys around.”
In that sense, Walker’s loss is no different from all the inevitable personnel changes that come during a regular season.
“There are guys that go in and out of your lineup for injury or other reasons,” Stefanski said, “so how you play could change a little bit game to game. That’s what we’re trying to do right now is find out a little bit about ourselves.”
Falcons coaches have acknowledged that they don’t have another player who can replicate the number of alignments in which Walker could be deployed.
“It was a huge deal because it allowed us to provide multiplicity. Where is Jalon going to be on this snap and this snap?” Timu said. “I think there are other guys who are a possibility, but it was tough news for us to lose him.”
The Falcons signed free agent Cameron Sample, a 2021 fourth-round pick by the Bengals who has seven sacks in four seasons, after Walker’s injury, and have enough roster and salary cap flexibility to make more moves at the position before the season begins. Other free agents currently available include Floyd, Haason Reddick, Joey Bosa, Derek Barnett and Yetur Gross-Matos. It’s also certain that Atlanta’s personnel department will pay close attention to players who become available when the other 31 teams trim their rosters at the end of the month.
The incumbent candidates to replace Walker’s production are newcomers Samson Ebukam, Azeez Ojulari, Cameron Thomas and Keshawn Banks and 2024 third-round pick Bralen Trice. Ebukam, Ojulari and Thomas all joined the team on one-year deals worth less than $3 million in the offseason.
Ebukam, an eight-year veteran, had a 9.5-sack season in 2023 with the Colts but missed all of 2024 due to an Achilles tear and returned to start one game last year. He has spent most of training camp with the first-team defense.
“Everybody has to be able to do their job,” Ebukam said. “We all play in the NFL. You have to go out there and compete, do (your) job the best (you) can do and let everything fall where it may.”
Ojulari is entering his sixth season but only played three games last year due to a hamstring injury. He has started 19 games over the last four seasons.
“I’m confident for sure,” Ojulari said. “You just have to put your head down, keep working, take it one day at a time. Do your job. … We all can rush the passer — just got to keep working every day. We’ve got to bring it.”
Thomas is a four-year veteran with three career starts. Banks is a former undrafted free agent who played most recently for the Orlando Storm of the UFL.
Trice may be the most intriguing player in the mix. He has missed both of his NFL seasons due to preseason ACL tears, but he has been a regular on the practice field throughout this offseason and training camp.
“I feel 100 percent comfortable out on the field,” Trice said. “I’ll be the same if not better just because I’ve had this time to figure out how I want to be on the field, how I want to take care of my body. That’s a huge part of the game.”
“Bralen is doing a nice job,” Stefanski said. “Looks healthy, very disruptive, powerful player. We will continue to bring him along and find his fit on the defense.”
Everyone in Atlanta’s rotation will be expected to expand their repertoire now, Timu said, but inside linebackers Kendal Daniels and Harold Perkins said they haven’t been approached about taking snaps outside.
“No matter who goes down, you have to be able to perform at the same level,” Ebukam said. “I know we’ve got pass rushers in the building, so that’s exactly what we’re going to do.”

title: Bills camp observations: Positive T.J. Sanders developments, Maxwell Hairston ramps up The Bills' preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers is just three days away. What's the latest from training camp? Joe Buscaglia 2

full_text:
T.J. Sanders, left, and Michael Hoecht are expected to be key players as the Buffalo Bills install a new defensive scheme. Joe Hrycych / Getty Images
The debut of the brand-new Buffalo Bills is fast approaching on Saturday afternoon. The Bills will unveil a new head coach, a new defense, a new defensive coordinator and a $2 billion new stadium in a game setting when they take on the Carolina Panthers at Highmark Stadium.
However, since head coach Joe Brady has been in Buffalo before, and the stadium got its curtain-opening night for the Return of the Blue & Red practice last weekend, the new-look defense might be the most intriguing part of the game. Defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard has put together plenty of different looks for the Bills’ new 3-4 defense through two weeks of training camp.
The Bills have been mixing and matching across all three levels of the defense to see what sticks. But on Saturday, Leonhard and the fanbase will finally get to see it live against someone other than their teammates.
“Anytime you get against different competition, things change,” Leonhard said Tuesday. “I am excited just to continue to push. We’ve only had so many days in pads, right? We’ve only had so many days where extended physical, you know, stress on these guys — whether it’s the play number or just the physicality of it. We’re going to continue to grow through this preseason.”
When asked about the idea of healthy defensive starters playing, Leonhard didn’t come right out and say it was happening, but he did push it in that direction.
“I think the plan is for guys to play and get a taste of the scheme live. Let’s go finish,” the defensive coordinator said. “As far as I’m concerned, guys are going to go play, to be determined a little bit on how much, but it’s going to be exciting for guys to get out there and just kind of let it rip.”
As the Bills get closer to that first taste of game action in a new defense, their players went through their first pair of practices at Orchard Park.
While plenty of defensive players have been getting the attention this summer through the new scheme, one relatively high-draft investment has slipped through the cracks a bit. Second-year defensive lineman T.J. Sanders has a potentially big role on the way despite limited action as a rookie, and the question is how he’ll respond to that enhanced opportunity. When asked about what they’ve seen and what they’d like to see more of, Leonhard was quick to point out how much they’ve put on Sanders’ plate.
“We’re asking him to play multiple roles,” Leonhard said. “We’re not just limiting him to one spot. So he’s moving to different areas of that defensive line, whether it’s our base package and our nickel package. So he is probably one of the guys who’s done the most and playing at a high level.”
Some of Sanders’ experience during his rookie season likely contributed to that versatility, as he played inside at defensive tackle and outside at defensive end when the Bills were dealing with numerous injuries in 2025. It’s unlikely that Sanders, at his weight (297 pounds), will play much nose tackle for the Bills, but lining up both on the inside shoulder of the offensive tackle and on the outside on other snaps gives him some different avenues to help bring him along as a pass rusher in game settings, which is what the Bills drafted him to do in the first place.
Leonhard also said Sanders has had to undergo the challenge of getting moved around more than his other defensive line teammates, so from a volume standpoint, he hasn’t had quite as many reps in one spot as some others. But more encouragingly, Leonhard also brought up the part of Sanders’ game that needed refinement.
“The physicality is improving,” Leonhard said. “What I’m seeing, like, he is committed to trying to be the physical player when he needs to be. Everybody knows he has some pass-rush ability and ability to get to the quarterback. And he’s flashed both. And again, now it’s just creating consistency.”
On the Bills’ first unofficial depth chart of the summer, Sanders was listed as one of their three starting defensive linemen in base formation. That is mostly consistent with how things have gone through camp and Sanders getting first-team time, so it seems as though the Bills are hoping for a big jump in Year 2 from their 2025 second-round pick.
The Bills have been without presumed starting No. 2 cornerback Maxwell Hairston for several practices, as he has missed time with an undisclosed injury. Throughout his time away, Hairston has been extremely visible during practices, often jogging up to celebrate with his cornerback teammates whenever they made a play against the opposition. That gave the sense that whatever he had been dealing with was never really a long-term concern. Those sentiments were backed up on Tuesday by Hairston being the first of the currently injured players to begin ramping up during practice.
After the Bills went into positional drills, Hairston emerged and went over to the side with some members of the strength and conditioning staff to begin some movement drills. Hairston was dressed in helmet and jersey, which is as good a sign as any.
Bills CB Maxwell Hairston starting to do some work along the side with athletic trainers. Ramping up, it appears. pic.twitter.com/rVrNpW8A86
— Joe Buscaglia (@JoeBuscaglia) August 11, 2026
Some of the drills focused on Hairston pushing off with his legs, which makes it most likely that he was dealing with a lower-body injury of some kind. At one point, Leonhard came over to check on Hairston before he got into the drills. Regardless, Hairston’s improvement is a big development for the Bills, who have some real questions with their cornerback depth as it stands. Even with rookie second-round pick Davison Igbinosun getting some more time working against the Bills’ top receivers, as it stands today, Hairston is fully expected to be the starter opposite No. 1 cornerback Christian Benford.
The Bills injury list had quite a handful of names with substantial roles on Tuesday. Along with the improving Hairston, the Bills were without starting center Connor McGovern, starting safeties Cole Bishop and C.J. Gardner-Johnson, third-down running back Ty Johnson and rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell. McGovern, Bishop, Johnson and Bell all haven’t been on the field since the team practiced inside the stadium on Saturday night, while Gardner-Johnson suffered an injury during Monday’s practice.
The Bills have not issued any update or timetable for any players to date, with Brady due to speak with reporters on Thursday morning.
McGovern’s injury looked like he was grabbing at his leg, though anything beyond that would be speculation. McGovern was not seen on the practice field during either of the last two practices. Teams are generally cautious with returning some of their bigger role players too early during the summer months, as there isn’t a game that counts for them until Sept. 13. In the meantime, expect to see plenty of backup center Lloyd Cushenberry III and backup safeties Geno Stone and Damar Hamlin.
The Bills also were without two of their more impressive undrafted rookies this summer, as cornerback Kani Walker and wide receiver Ja’Mori Maclin did not participate on Tuesday.
With Reggie Gilliam’s departure via free agency this offseason, it opened up a job for someone new to take over the primary fullback role within the Bills’ offense. The team elected to bring on a competition between a low-cost veteran on a one-year deal against an undrafted rookie free agent. That veteran was Ben VanSumeren, whose 2025 season ended abruptly in Week 1 with a torn patellar tendon. Through the early stages of camp, whenever the Bills worked a fullback into the first-team looks of 11-on-11, VanSumeren was the one taking the reps.
Over the last two practices, that has changed, as rookie Jackson Acker — an athletic prospect out of Wisconsin — began working in with Josh Allen and company.…

title: Exclusive: Spending a day with Bears coach Ben Johnson at training camp He doesn't just want a Super Bowl. He wants to leave no doubt. "I want shutouts. I want blowouts. I want the highest-scoring offense ever." Dan Pompei 2
summary:
After winning the North in his first season as a head coach last year, Ben Johnson has higher aspirations. Much higher. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; photo: Icon Sportswire / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — It’s shortly before 5 a.m. on Aug. 4, and the Chicago Bears offices are dark.
Then Ben Johnson walks into his suite, and there is light.
But energy, too, definitely energy.
There is enough to light his office and more, enough to make a great city shine a little more brightly.
full_text:
After winning the North in his first season as a head coach last year, Ben Johnson has higher aspirations. Much higher. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; photo: Icon Sportswire / Getty Images
LAKE FOREST, Ill. — It’s shortly before 5 a.m. on Aug. 4, and the Chicago Bears offices are dark.
Then Ben Johnson walks into his suite, and there is light.
But energy, too, definitely energy.
There is enough to light his office and more, enough to make a great city shine a little more brightly.
Johnson shows up neither with sleep in the corners of his eyes nor bags beneath them. He removes his Chicago Blackhawks cap and replaces it with a retro B Bears logo cap as Vance Joy plays. There is no yawn in his song.
He usually gets five hours of sleep this time of year, and that suffices. Johnson can function with four, which he normally settles for once the games begin. His alarm is set for 4:30, but he usually wakes well before then, thinking about how his Chicago Bears can redefine greatness.
The Bears’ head coach is amped about today’s practice, more so than usual because there will be two live periods — the first time his team will play real football since its playoff loss to the Los Angeles Rams last January. Last night, he made it understood to coaches, offensive players and defensive ones that chinstraps had best be buckled because he will be setting a tone by calling mostly runs.
Many NFL coaches don’t go live anymore, but Johnson learned from Dan Campbell when he was Campbell’s offensive coordinator with the Detroit Lions. And besides, if Campbell is going live, Johnson believes the Bears need to do the same if they want to finish ahead of the Lions in the NFC North.
After winning the North in his first season as a head coach last year, Johnson has higher aspirations. Much higher.
“You’ve got 31 other teams coming to training camp saying, ‘Our goal is to win the Super Bowl,'” he says. “I want more than that. I want to have the highest-scoring offense ever, which happens to be the 2013 Denver Broncos. I know how many points per game they scored (37.9), and I want to surpass them. I want shutouts. I want blowouts.”
He asks which team has the most consecutive victories. It’s the New England Patriots, who won 21 straight between 2003 and 2004.
“Why can’t we do that?” he says. “There has never been an undefeated season (since teams have been playing more than 14 regular-season games). The moon is the Super Bowl, but we’re shooting beyond that, for the stars. And I want these players to feel that each and every single day they come in.”
Assuredly they do. As does everyone else in his presence at Halas Hall, which, on this day, includes a reporter.
On a 14-hour training camp day, The Athletic shadowed the fascinating Ben Johnson.
In the private locker room in his office, Johnson changes into workout gear. He does 12 warm-up push-ups before heading downstairs.
Anyone who has felt the laser-beam stare will tell you about his intensity.
You can see it on the fleshy part of his left hand, where there is a lump that came from rubbing it with his right thumb. His mother sends him stress balls that he bounces and squeezes throughout the day. Bears cornerback Tyrique Stevenson gave him a fidget spinner.
That intensity is clear after games, whether he is brushing past the opposing coach who happens to work on the wrong side of the state border, or galvanizing his troops with a “Good, better, best!” speech . It was especially plain to see in his performance after a November victory over the Philadelphia Eagles, when he removed his shirt, which meant free hot dogs in Chicago.
If the giveaway glizzies weren’t part of the deal, we never would have been exposed to Johnson’s washboard, he says. He was uncomfortable with the spotlight he found himself in, but he understands the value of sharing on ChicagoBears.com.
“The No. 1 thing is we are here to win,” he says. “But we’re also a part of the entertainment industry. And I think part of what we sign up for with these jobs is doing things for our fanbase, getting them excited about what we are doing. That goes into why we do some things that might sparkle and shine on game day, things that draw attention to our guys in a positive way that our fans can enjoy.”
There is no better place to feel the Johnson intensity than in the Clyde Emrich Weight Room at Halas Hall. He starts with 15 minutes of intervals on a treadmill and follows with 30 minutes of weight training. With Bears strength coach Pierre Ngo’s guidance, Johnson focuses on Olympic lifts — power cleans, squats and bench press. Today, he gets up to six reps with 250 pounds on the bench. The other day, he squatted 400 pounds.
He’s been working out six days a week, and he’s as strong as he’s been since he was a walk-on quarterback at North Carolina 20 years ago. Once the games begin, he will cut back to two workouts a week when the Bears are at home and one workout when they’re on the road.
By January, he usually loses about 10 pounds. But since he gifted Chicago with those hot dogs, Johnson has put on 10 pounds, and they are good pounds.
He won’t be taking off his shirt again, he says. But just in case, he gets in some bicycle crunches.
Johnson sits in a quiet area of the cafeteria with scrambled eggs and a biscuit, both covered in gravy, and a bowl of fruit. The sprint to the end of the season has begun, and he won’t have many opportunities for reflection. This is one of them.
It was a different year than any that preceded it for Johnson. He was a finalist for NFL Coach of the Year in February, but he turned down an invitation to attend NFL Honors in San Francisco.
Instead, he, his wife, Jessica, and their daughters, Emory, 9, and Halle, 3, and son Kennedy, 7, went to Fort Lauderdale, Fla. He and Jessica turned 40 in May, so in June, the couple went to California’s wine country, their first vacation alone since Emory was born. The family also spent time in North Carolina, where Ben and Jessica have roots. Mostly, though, they enjoyed the Chicago area, hanging at a coffee shop and a North Shore beach on Saturday mornings.
Johnson may be a rock star to Bears fans, but he hasn’t had to go incognito like one because he blends in easily among the people. In June, he attended a bachelor party weekend in Chicago for Connor Barth, his teammate at North Carolina and a former Bears kicker. He left Barth and their friends in the afternoon and walked from the Chicago River to Soldier Field to meet some of his assistants for a Morgan Wallen concert. Johnson went unrecognized until just before he entered the stadium.
Ted Crews, special adviser to the president, apologizes for interrupting breakfast. He explains that defensive coordinator Dennis Allen is meeting the media soon, and it is expected he will be asked about safety Coby Bryant, who left practice injured the day before. No one from the team has given a status update on Bryant, but it has been reported he will miss eight to 10 weeks. Crews and Johnson discuss how Allen should handle inquiries, agreeing he should avoid specifics.
Crews leaves, and Johnson takes a bite of eggs.
It’s clear that all the planets at Halas Hall revolve around Johnson. He could act like a king, but Johnson is approachable to the point that cafeteria workers feel comfortable small-talking with him. And when he converses with them, he is fully present.
A lesson in humility from 2019 stays with Johnson. During a good run as an assistant with the Dolphins, he thought the arrow was pointing up on his career. Then he was a casualty of a regime change. He was out of work for seven months — the worst time of his life, he calls it.
Now, Johnson understands that one day, his corner office overlooking the practice fields will have another nameplate outside of it, and all he has worked for will be gone. So he’s determined to give whatever he can while he can.
“I’m completely happy with the thought that this is my last job,” he says. “It’s the best job…

full_text:
Cashius Howell has made an impression on coaches and his fellow teammates in training camp. Frank Bowen IV / The Enquirer / USA Today via Reuters Connect
CINCINNATI — One year ago, development of the Cincinnati Bengals’ rookie class was directly tied to the results of the season. The six-pick class started a combined 53 games, with everyone except sixth-round running back Tahj Brooks starting at least five.
Cincinnati lived — and eventually died — by its growing pains.
That’s not the case this year with the Bengals’ seven-man class not currently projecting a single starter on the veteran squad.
Coach Zac Taylor started his assessment of this class by saying “nobody feels out of place” and that they have handled the mental aspect of the game well, with each competing for roles behind the starters.
But in terms of feeling less pressure with this group to develop quickly compared to last year filling more prominent roles, no, that’s not the case in the least.
“No, because you never know when it can come up, where they’re needed immediately,” he said. “And so that’s always in the back of a coach’s mind is they may be viewed as a depth player or backup, but we all know they’ve got to be ready in a moment’s notice. And so you always have that urgency to make sure that they’re ready to go. So I don’t ever feel the easing in, we’re not counting on this guy, so we can be a little more patient with them. Usually, feels the opposite.”
The urgency will be on the mind of the head coach and evaluators when the rookies make their NFL debuts Thursday against Detroit.
These seven will be building on the foundation of 10 practices. Here’s a broader view of how the 10 practices went for each draft pick, their projected roles, key quotes, notable plays, analysis and first-impression grades.
Role: Second-team edge rusher with a rotational role as outside linebacker on passing downs.
Play that stands out: On Thursday, Howell earned his first 11-on-11 reps against the starting offensive line. On his debut against Orlando Brown Jr. at left tackle, Howell went bull rush under the chin and drove the veteran back, planting him at the feet of Joe Burrow. The hit was benefited by Brown’s foot getting caught on running back Samaje Perine, but that was partially due to the initial drive he put on the 350-pound Brown.
Later in the same session, he used his patented lateral burst and bend around the edge to dip around Brown and past Burrow’s back. Howell’s speed and power on his first foray against the ones lifted the ceiling on his instant-impact potential.
Key quote: Myles Murphy on Howell finding his comfort level: “Whatever he’s doing, something’s working.”
Analysis: Howell will be part of the rotation in Week 1. There’s too much juice off the edge for that not to be the case. The reigning SEC Defensive Player of the Year will be the ultimate chess piece defensive coordinator Al Golden will have to decide how to use. How often will he have Howell drop in coverage? He’s been working on that during portions of camp. Will he be specific to 3-4 looks or carve out a piece of the nickel defense? His reps have mostly been limited to the second team, so how he performs against the starters will go a long way.
Inevitably, Golden wants this line to come in waves, and Howell bringing his pass-rush ability fresh off the bench will be a weapon, specifically if the Bengals are trying to close out a win.
First-impression grade: B. On par with expectations to this point. The pleasant surprise has been his physicality, which caught the eye of the coaching staff (and Brown) as the pads went on.
Role: Fourth cornerback, solely playing outside.
Play that stands out: On the first day in pads, Joe Flacco tried to hit Colbie Young deep down the sideline. Young has made a habit of winning contested catches during this camp, but with the ball slightly underthrown, Davis was able to extend, break up the pass and nearly pull down the pick. That’s the first spot where his 80 7/8-inch wing span — longest among drafted corners — really showed up.
Key quote: Davis on his first camp, including competition against Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins: “It’s a blessing to be going against the best duo in the whole world and Joe Burrow. I couldn’t ask for a better position than this. It don’t get no better than this.”
Analysis: Preseason games will go a long way to determining Davis’ current level. He’s been steady through 10 practices. You don’t notice him getting burnt routinely. He also hasn’t made a pile of splash plays. He notched his first interception on Friday and appears to be gaining confidence. He hasn’t challenged DJ Ivey for the third cornerback spot, but that was expected considering the learning curve.
First-impression grade: C+. On par with expectations. Davis won’t be needed to play immediately, barring injury, but laid a solid foundation through 10 days.
Play that stands out: Lew stepped in with the first team on Tuesday for the first time. There was one bad snap in his first real work with Burrow, but overall the drive going as normal was a victory for the rookie coming off a torn ACL.
Key quote: Lew on how he feels progressing back from his injury: “A really good collaboration between us, especially this return-to-play process. We started with maybe three reps one day, OK, how did that feel? Just really building day by day. It’s felt really good. I haven’t had any problems putting any weight on it or anything like that. So we’ll just keep going.”
Analysis: Lew won’t play Thursday, but all signs have been good about his ability to be active when the season starts. Opting to give him a drive with the first team Tuesday was a positive sign about belief in where he’s at from a health and talent standpoint.
First-impression grade: B. Just being in the mix and handling the mental and physical load is a positive considering he’s coming off a major injury.
Role: Competing for a spot in the pecking order behind Chase and Higgins.
Play that stands out: Young might have the best catch of camp. The 6-foot-4, 218-pound rookie went up in double coverage and hauled in a deep ball from Flacco last week. He’s become a consistent jump-ball winner, snagging at least one contested catch in nearly every practice over the last week.
Key quote: Young on the impact he’s felt from stacking days with flash plays. “When I get in that huddle (the quarterback) looks over and knows he’s got a guy he can put it up there for a 70-30 ball, in my eyes.”
Analysis: Young established one truth through 10 days: He can go get it. That’s a delightful trait to own, especially at his size. It also won’t dictate how much playing time he receives this year. Young will be judged by his ability to block in the run game, understand the system and find separation when given an opportunity. It’s extremely hard to see him topping Andrei Iosivas and all his experience in that regard. Could he top Mitch Tinsley for next in line? That will be determined over the next three weeks.
First-impression grade: B. The size and contested catch ability are alluring, but he needs to show consistent separation in his routes and build his understanding of the system.
Role: Second-team interior offensive line.
Play that stands out: Parker has played all three positions across the interior thus far. One of his best plays came on the second day in pads, leading the way on a draw for Perine and standing up linebacker Oren Burks in the hole, clearing the way for an explosive run.
Key quote: Parker on his adjustment from playing tackle at Duke to interior O-line for the Bengals: “Everything happens a lot faster on the inside, so I’m getting used to that. As we’ve been going, I’ve been getting more comfortable. Mentally, I got the playbook down. Now it is focusing on physical traits and technique to get me to the next level.”
Analysis: Parker has shown flashes, but he’ll require patience in his development as he moves inside for the first time. He’s searching…

full_text:
Deshaun Watson and Shedeur Sanders headline the biggest remaining NFL quarterback competitions. Nick Cammett / Getty Images
The first major quarterback battle of NFL training camp season has reportedly been decided with the Minnesota Vikings naming Kyler Murray the starter ahead of J.J. McCarthy , but more competitions are unfolding across the league.
The Cleveland Browns, Atlanta Falcons and Las Vegas Raiders have yet to announce a Week 1 starter – though markets have crowned clear favorites in each race. Let’s start with the tightest of the three.
Could the starting position in Cleveland be destined for another revolving door? Traders on Kalshi have their money on Deshaun Watson edging Shedeur Sanders out for those rights come Week 1, at least.
Coach Todd Monken muddied the waters when he handed Watson the keys to the No. 1 offense on Saturday before returning them to Sanders on Monday, and as The Athletic ’s Zac Jackson wrote in a detailed account of the battle earlier this week, it’s not yet clear which (if either) quarterback is pulling away. The first-year head coach maintains he envisions that each will start one of the team’s first two preseason games: at the Chicago Bears this Saturday, then vs. the Buffalo Bills on Aug. 22.
Sanders started the final seven games of last season after taking over for Dillon Gabriel, who had been promoted over Joe Flacco before that. Gabriel went 1-5 in his six starts; Sanders went 3-4 in his seven.
More than $200,000 has been exchanged to make it the most popular of the QB battle markets. Who would start for the Minnesota Vikings was the second-most popular with just shy of $140,000 traded on a market that positioned Kyler Murray as an 81 percent favorite before The Athletic reported the team was moving forward with Murray over J.J. McCarthy.
The Athletic ’s Josh Kendall described the Falcons’ quarterback situation as “a mess” earlier this week, but that hasn’t stopped traders from buying Tua Tagovailoa as the lead man in Atlanta.
The Miami Dolphins benched Tagovailoa in the final three weeks of last season after he threw a career-high 15 interceptions in 14 starts. He has also been dealing with back tightness during camp. Still, with Michael Penix Jr. (left ACL) yet to be cleared for 11-on-11 work, the market believes this is Tagovailoa’s job to lose, at least to start the season.
A little more than $20,000 has been traded on this outcome so far.
Fernando Mendoza took the reigns of the No. 1 offense for the first time on Saturday when Kirk Cousins was held out of practice after getting in a scuffle with teammate Maxx Crosby on Friday, but those reps have otherwise belonged to the veteran Cousins.
The Raiders’ unofficial depth chart for Thursday’s preseason opener against the Arizona Cardinals lists Cousins as the QB1 and Mendoza as the QB2. Traders on Kalshi are banking on that holding, with Cousins holding a clear edge over the No. 1 draft pick in a market that has taken more than $25,000 in positions.

full_text:
Cowboys QB Dak Prescott felt good about the team's performance Tuesday in a joint practice with the Rams. Kirby Lee / Imagn Images
WOODLAND HILLS, Calif. — The Dallas Cowboys’ starters aren’t expected to play in the preseason. Their best work to get ready for Week 1 is likely to come in their joint training camp practices with the Los Angeles Rams and New Orleans Saints. They had one of those sessions Tuesday as they traveled to the Rams practice facility in Woodland Hills.
The Cowboys arrived around 9:30 a.m. PT, and things ended around noon. There wasn’t much individual work. There was no seven-on-seven. The teams basically got right into team drills with the Rams’ offense and Cowboys’ defense on one field and the Cowboys’ offense and the Rams’ defense on the other. The team-drill portion was broken down into three segments with special teams work in between.
We were not permitted to record video of the team-drill portion. Here are the highlights.
• The first-team offense was very good in red zone work. Dak Prescott had two touchdown passes to CeeDee Lamb, one to KaVontae Turpin and another to tight end Brevyn Spann-Ford. The best highlight of the four was probably a back-shoulder throw to Lamb. Prescott also had a touchdown pass on a slant to Ryan Flournoy.
That’s one of the biggest areas the Cowboys need to improve on from a year ago. The extra work they’ve been putting in during camp practices appears to be paying off.
“I think that was probably the stronger drill or the stronger period of the day for us, and so that’s good,” Prescott said after practice. “Obviously coming off of the struggles at the end of last year, it’s good to see. Even though we’ve got things in our back pocket that obviously we’re not going pull out just yet, so most definitely.”
• George Pickens continued to be the star of stars. He’s had an excellent camp, and that continued with multiple catches, including a nice back-shoulder grab along the right sideline and a slant he took in for a score.
“That’s just George being George,” Prescott said. “That’s what I expect from him. That’s what he expects from himself. There’s still probably a ball or two that we want to correct.”
Prescott had one interception while targeting Pickens in the end zone.
“(That one) can get cleaned up very simply,” Prescott said. “(That practice) is what I expect from George. He just does great things, and today was another showing of that.”
• Joe Milton was the second-team quarterback. He had a solid day with one interception that came on a highlight leaping grab by a Rams linebacker as Milton was moving to his left.
• Offensive coordinator Klayton Adams called the offense while Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer bounced back and forth between the fields.
• It was not a great day for right tackle Terence Steele. He had issues in pass protection going against Rams outside linebacker Byron Young. Rams star edge rusher Myles Garrett did not participate in the practice. He watched from the sideline.
• Tyler Guyton spent time with the trainers looking at his arm but he returned and appeared to have a good day.
• Starting running back Javonte Williams probably had his best run in the second team-drill period. It came on a handoff he took to the left, running behind Tyler Smith and Guyton. There was no tackling to the ground, but the play would have likely gone for more than 10 yards.
• No. 2 running back Jaydon Blue lost a fumble on a carry during the first team-drill period.
• Working with the third team, Sam Howell had a touchdown pass to rookie tight end Michael Trigg.
The Cowboys have been running after practice to help improve their conditioning. Some Rams players cracked jokes about it as they exited the fields after practice, which led to some spirited trash talk between the teams. Schottenheimer said the usual running was the idea of the players, not the coaching staff. “We’ve got the right guys,” he added. “The leaders of this football team are some of our best players. Historically, that usually means you’re gonna have a lot of success.”
• Dallas’ defense was destroyed by the Rams’ offense when the teams practiced together last year. And Los Angeles was without MVP QB Matthew Stafford. The Cowboys faced Stafford on Tuesday, and they had a much better showing this time. Stafford connected on a few big plays, but that’s to be expected from him and their talented offense.
“We’re a different defense,” Schottenheimer said after practice. “You guys know that. You can look at us on paper and see we’re a different defense. Having practiced against (our offense) every day the mentality and mindset of the defense is different. I think that’s great. (The Rams) challenge you in a lot of different ways. They’re a very, very physical run team. … Matthew Stafford has an unbelievable ability to get the ball out of his hand fast, so they’re hard to get home on.
“But a few guys jumped out today. Quinnen Williams, I think we should probably keep that contract. I think that’s a good contract for us. Thrilled about him. … I thought it was a battle. They had their plays, we had our plays. It’s what a joint practice should look like.”
• Williams was arguably Dallas’ best defender on the day, causing plenty of problems in the run and pass game up the middle.
• Backup linebacker Justin Barron had the most highlights of anyone, recording three interceptions. One came off Stafford and the other two were on throws from Rams backup QB Stetson Bennett.
• Donovan Ezeiruaku was noticeable, especially early with a sack and a nice run stop.
• Caleb Downs had an impressive tackle for loss on a run play and was active all over the field. He was working more at safety as Malik Hooker did not practice for personal reasons.
• Shavon Revel continued to build on his strong camp. He nearly intercepted Stafford on a well-defended fade ball in the end zone. Cobie Durant also recorded a pass breakup.
• DeMarvion Overshown continued to move around well. Dee Winters continued to make plays at the other linebacker spot. Those two remain the expected starting linebackers Week 1.
“It’s just showing what we’ve been building on from the spring up until now,” Overshown said after practice. “It was good to hit a different color jersey. … Getting to see what we got against another top offense, it puts stuff in perspective. Just another block that we’re building on.”

title: What's next for J.J. McCarthy after Vikings name Kyler Murray the starting QB? Will the 23-year-old first-round pick from 2024 be happy as Minnesota's backup, or might the Vikings be better off trading him? Alec Lewis 2
summary:

EAGAN, Minn. — This journey began in January. The 2025 season had just ended, and Minnesota Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell said “there has to be” competition at the quarterback position.
That incited an extensive evaluation of the free-agent QB class by the offensive staff. The Vikings left the combine in Indianapolis with t
full_text:
Third-year quarterback J.J. McCarthy's up-and-down performances in training camp made Kyler Murray coach Kevin O'Connell's choice as the starter. David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — This journey began in January. The 2025 season had just ended, and Minnesota Vikings coach Kevin O’Connell said “there has to be” competition at the quarterback position.
That incited an extensive evaluation of the free-agent QB class by the offensive staff. The Vikings left the combine in Indianapolis with their priorities set, and veteran Kyler Murray sat atop the list.
Murray’s signing in mid-March gave O’Connell a chance to name a starter, but he declined. Instead, for months, he insisted there would be a competition between Murray and 2024 first-round pick J.J. McCarthy. The thought was the challenge and shared discomfort would enhance the play of both quarterbacks, and, by extension, the entire offense.
Locker room leaders publicly backed the strategy, even though people around the league — including some Vikings staffers and players — fully expected Tuesday’s outcome all along.
In the morning, O’Connell met with both quarterbacks and informed them Murray would be the starter . Then, after a team meeting and a walk-through, O’Connell explained the decision to reporters, focusing on Murray’s experience and potential.
“I think the competition benefitted both of those guys,” O’Connell said, “and maybe accelerated some things, and maybe also let us know exactly where we’re at with both guys in our attempt to get them both ready.”
This long-awaited anointment shifts the conversation forward. The discussion moves from “How did the two quarterbacks look today?” to “What is Murray capable of in O’Connell’s revamped system?”
But there’s another question that’s worth asking, too. What does Tuesday’s news mean for McCarthy?
O’Connell said Tuesday that McCarthy will be the Vikings’ backup and the 23-year-old will continue to receive significant reps.
“We want to be absolutely mindful not only of where he’s at right now,” O’Connell said, “but also where we think he can get by the start of the season. We’ve learned over the years that we don’t hold the cards. We need as many guys (as possible) to be comfortable and ready.”
Eight quarterbacks have started games for the Vikings since the 2023 season began. The quarterback carousel has torpedoed two of the last three seasons. With those harrowing memories in mind, the franchise loaded up at the position this offseason. Murray’s addition produced the headlines. Re-signing veteran Carson Wentz not only generated more insurance, but it also opened the door to a glut of depth that could precede a trade.
It is well known around the league McCarthy’s play in 2025 wore on O’Connell and the offensive staff. Inaccuracies complicated routine throws. Extra hitches threw off the timing of pass concepts. Struggles applying touch on throws to areas of the field limited the team’s offensive menu. On top of all of that, McCarthy’s high ankle sprain and hand injuries shattered any positive momentum.
The numbers paint the most objective picture. Among the 36 quarterbacks who threw at least 200 passes in 2025, McCarthy ranked 34th in efficiency, 35th in completion percentage and 36th in touchdown-to-interception ratio. His struggles forced O’Connell to simplify the offense and call plays with a conservative mindset.
These dynamics sent Minnesota down the Murray path.
In the spring, McCarthy initially described the pairing as being like two high schoolers sitting on opposite sides of the classroom. This summer, when asked whether he’d thought about the possibility of a trade, McCarthy said, “I think I made it very clear I wanted to be here before I got here. I love this organization. I love the coaching staff. I absolutely love these players to death. This is where I want to be.”
Tuesday’s announcement creates another layer to consider. The Vikings value a positive environment within the quarterbacks group, especially given O’Connell’s history as a player and coach at the position. Simultaneously, McCarthy and his camp must assess whether this situation with the Vikings is the most advantageous for his future.
Comparable circumstances with other first-round picks who have been benched don’t provide a simple answer. Last fall, the Indianapolis Colts benched Anthony Richardson, who later requested a trade. He remains on the roster. Conversely, the San Francisco 49ers transitioned away from Trey Lance after two seasons by trading him to the Dallas Cowboys for a fourth-round pick.
It remains unclear what the Vikings might net for McCarthy in a trade.
Despite the rumors of a potential deal, O’Connell said Tuesday he “absolutely” sees McCarthy as still having a future with the organization. He cited McCarthy’s improvement in training camp as a reason for optimism. He also mentioned McCarthy’s need to stay ready in case he’s needed in a pinch.
“As he knows, he’s holding the pen on his story,” O’Connell said. “We’re going to support him and try to help him continue to improve as a young player at the most difficult position in sports.”
McCarthy did not speak to reporters after Tuesday’s announcement. He is expected to offer his perspective Wednesday.

full_text:
Even in a crowded Jets tight end room, Jelani Woods has carved out a likely role. Adam Hunger / AP
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — The moment was small enough that most people didn’t notice — or, maybe, care. It was a minute detail toward the end of a miserable New York Jets season, occurring late in another blowout loss. A Jets tight end lined up on the left side of the line of scrimmage. When quarterback Brady Cook took the snap, the tight end blocked a New England Patriots linebacker before leaking across the middle. Cook found him. The tight end caught the ball as he fell to the ground.
And then life went on. It registered as a 4-yard reception in the box score. But for Jelani Woods, it was much more.
“It was meaningful,” Woods said, his large frame — 6-foot-7, 253 pounds, 83-inch wingspan — crowding a small chair at the Jets facility after a recent practice.
Woods went 1,085 days between catches. Injuries robbed him of two full seasons with the Indianapolis Colts, stalling what was an otherwise promising start to his career. His athletic testing leading up to the 2022 NFL Draft was historic — according to one measurement , it was the most impressive testing for any tight end prospect since at least 1987. But despite a 4.61-second 40-yard dash and 37.5-inch vertical leap, Woods couldn’t outrun or out-jump the imbalance in his body. A hamstring strain cost him one season. Turf toe cost him another. Two full seasons, and most of a third, without playing a football game that counted.
Woods had to relearn his body. Specialists discovered things he was doing, or not doing, that could have contributed to his injuries. He changed his regimen, his workouts and his approach to fitness. It wasn’t until he walked through the doors at the Jets facility for the first time, after the Colts gave up on him, that he started to feel like himself again.
Now, he’s thriving. Last week, he caught a touchdown toward the end of an intrasquad scrimmage. Quarterback Geno Smith recently was asked to name someone on offense who had surprised him. The quarterback’s answer: Jelani Woods.
“I like the way he’s been making plays,” Smith said.
Jets coach Aaron Glenn lights up when he talks about Woods. He’s played his way into a role in a new Jets offense that is going to emphasize the tight end position. If he was on the bubble to make the team at the start of training camp, he isn’t anymore.
“It’s training camp. It seems hard, but just going through the past two, three years makes me appreciate waking up in the morning like, all right, I got another opportunity to just get better,” Woods said. “You appreciate it way more. So, on days like today, when you’re just grinding — you gotta love it. I’ve got a whole different mindset now.”
Woods has found his place, and his peace. All it took was his body feeling like it was in one piece.
Woods returned to the Jets facility in March to re-sign with the team that claimed him off waivers last summer. As he walked through to the coaches offices, he saw Glenn first. The coach saw him and smiled; the two have developed a bond. Woods kept walking, heading to meet new tight ends coach Alfredo Roberts for the first time. But Frank Reich’s office comes first in the hallway.
Woods and Reich locked eyes. They both smiled. Reich “shot up” out of his seat, Woods said, and yelled: “JELANI!”
They hugged “for a good little minute”, Woods said, and then Frank, jubilant, told him: “Man, I’m so glad to have you back!”
“It was just big smiles,” Woods said. “And it’s been like that every day since.”
“Yeah,” Reich said recently, “I love Jelani.”
Woods always wanted to come back to the Jets — he felt a connection to this team and the organization. But Glenn hiring Reich as his new offensive coordinator in February sealed it.
“I was like, I’m there,” Woods said. “Ain’t no ifs, ands or buts about it. I didn’t even need to think about it.”
Reich was the head coach of the Colts when they selected Woods in the third round of 2022 draft. The last time Woods felt like himself was when Reich was coaching him, pushing him. “He was on me my rookie year,” Woods said. “That helped me big time because it helped me understand: This is the NFL.”
Their time together didn’t last as long as either had hoped. Woods had 312 receiving yards and three touchdowns as a rookie, but Reich was fired midway through the year. Woods flashed even after Reich was gone; there was optimism that he’d take the next step in 2023. Then he pulled his hamstring in OTAs, aggravated it during training camp and tore his other hamstring before the season started. His second year ended before it started, and he’s never been the same since.
In the 2024 preseason, Woods suffered a turf toe injury that required surgery and sidelined him for another full season. NFL players who suffer season-ending injuries often talk about how isolating that can be — spending so much time in rehab, away from your teammates, alone. Instead of falling into that, Woods stayed active in the tight end room. His brother, Jaleel, moved into his apartment so he wasn’t alone on the days when it felt that way. And then he worked to find out what was wrong, why these injuries kept happening.
“It was actually crazy because I started feeling like myself again” in 2024, he said. “I had to knock the rust off and, you know, deal with being scared about the hamstring stuff and trying to get over that. When I finally felt like I got over it — then that (turf toe) happened. It was just like, oh my gosh, OK, what am I doing wrong? What am I not paying attention to?”
He met with various specialists and arrived at a conclusion: Without realizing it, Woods’ body was unbalanced. Whether because of his injuries or his long legs and limbs, Woods was overcompensating in some areas. One side of his body was stronger than the other, and the way he was working out and lifting weights only intensified that.
“It was just learning my body because I’m kind of not normal,” Woods said. “I had to balance things out and learn my body — the whole body is a chain. So I saw the specialists to see where my weaknesses are, how it’s related to where my strengths are and to try to get it to balance out.”
Woods learned that some parts of his body were “way stronger” than the others, which is why he was “overcompensating in some ways.” The injuries exacerbated that — a calf strain left him putting more weight on his foot, which likely contributed to the turf toe.
“There’s so much that went into it that I didn’t know at the time,” Woods said.
He worked with a physical therapist who helped him discover areas of tightness on his lower body that he’d never noticed before. His new workout plan involved isolated exercises. An example: instead of doing regular squats, Woods does split squats to give each side of his body equal footing. When he used to work out, he’d favor his stronger side without realizing it — and he lifted a lot of weight, too. “You do it so often and it (your body) can get out of whack,” Woods said. “And then you train hard, you do it over a set amount of times, your balance is off and then that can lead to injuries.”
The new approach seems to be working.
Said Roberts: “I just want him to have some luck.”
Woods said he felt like “himself” the moment he joined the Jets after training camp last season, though he didn’t really get the chance to show it on Sundays. He didn’t play in a game until Week 8, when he played one snap, and then not again until Week 15. But Woods didn’t even mind — he was centrally focused on staying healthy for a whole season. He was happy to grind out reps on the scout team — at least he was playing football.
“I know the talent is there, so it was just about staying healthy and proving that I can stay healthy,” Woods said. “I felt like I got a lot of opportunities, even in practice, to showcase what I can do. That was my biggest thing: Show them who I really am, because they don’t really know.”
He still played enough to etch himself in…

title: NFL offenses battled the play clock more than ever last year. The Eagles could buck the trend The Eagles are shifting away from the slow pre-snap approach that defined their 2025 season. Brooks Kubena
summary:
The Philadelphia Eagles led the NFL with 150 last-second plays under former offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — The Philadelphia Eagles topped a leaguewide trend during the 2025 season in which NFL offenses experienced a massive spike in the number of plays that begin close to the expiration of the play clock.
The trend did not suit the Eagles — nor their former offensive coordinator, Kevin Patullo, who was fired after his first season as play caller.
full_text:
The Philadelphia Eagles led the NFL with 150 last-second plays under former offensive coordinator Kevin Patullo. Mitchell Leff / Getty Images
PHILADELPHIA — The Philadelphia Eagles topped a leaguewide trend during the 2025 season in which NFL offenses experienced a massive spike in the number of plays that begin close to the expiration of the play clock.
The trend did not suit the Eagles — nor their former offensive coordinator, Kevin Patullo, who was fired after his first season as play caller. Now, under another first-time coordinator, Sean Mannion, the Eagles are shifting away from a slow pre-snap approach that several players likened to playing chess, and toward a style that aims to make them the aggressor.
“This offense is really just about being quick, getting to the ball and running our plays,” said left guard Landon Dickerson, a six-year veteran and three-time Pro Bowler. “I think for us, it’s sometimes you want to overthink things — not in a bad way. But in the system we were in before, it was kind of problem-solving once we got to the line of scrimmage. This just lets us get up there and play ball fast.”
The 2025 Eagles led the NFL with a style of play that to the layman’s eye can seem like lollygagging. The Eagles, who never totaled more than 37 plays snapped with one second left on the play clock in a given season under previous play callers Kellen Moore, Brian Johnson and Shane Steichen, led the league with 150 last-second plays under Patullo. The league average of plays with one second left on the play clock skyrocketed from 20.9 in 2024 to 73.2 in 2025, according to TruMedia.
The league average hadn’t been greater than 23.4 since 2019. (The league average of total plays with three seconds or less also surged from 114.5 in 2024 to 200.9 in 2025.)
There is a leading explanation for the surge, according to several coaches: Defensive play callers have been increasingly effective at disguising their coverages, and offenses adjusted by spending more time decoding at the line of scrimmage. That five teams other than the Eagles soared above 100 last-second plays in 2025 (the Pittsburgh Steelers, Jacksonville Jaguars, Buffalo Bills, Green Bay Packers and Carolina Panthers) builds the case for leaguewide heavy-thinking. Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, widely renowned for masking his coverages, said he has noticed teams trying to “get into the perfect play” and subsequently running into the play clock.
“Long gone are the days where you get very clear man-zone indicators, you get very clear one-high or two-high pressure-triggers,” said Panthers offensive coordinator Brad Idzik, who is taking over the play-calling from coach Dave Canales this season. “Defenses do such a good job of making it muddy pre-snap that I think a lot of teams are just trying to absorb as much info as they can to see if they can get a bead on what the defense is doing.
“I know our defense does a phenomenal job of it,” Idzik added. “And that’s why we have to press on our end the urgency of getting to the line of scrimmage, the urgency of, if we have a motion, there’s a reason for it to try to get the defense to undress as fast as possible so we’re not up against the clock. That is definitely a huge trend that we keep track of. And we don’t want to be on the back end of snapping that thing with one second every time because that’ll be the O-lineman’s worst friend, when the defensive line knows, ‘OK, they either snap it now, or they’re a delay of game.’ (The defense) can roar off the ball. We wanna stay ahead of the clock and continue to be in an attacking nature as much as we can.”
Idzik is not alone in highlighting one solution: Get to the line of scrimmage faster. NFL teams broke the huddle 1.3 seconds later in 2025 than they did in 2024. The Eagles averaged 19.1 seconds left on the play clock when breaking the huddle in 2025, down from 20.4 in 2024. The little time they had left, plus the time they spent decoding defenses, compounded the disadvantages of an offensive system that was sometimes predictable . Mannion said it is a “huge” priority this year for the coaching staff to monitor defensive personnel, manage substitutions and get plays in quickly to give quarterback Jalen Hurts and the offense more time at the line.
“It’s critical,” Mannion said. “We want to apply pressure to the defense at all times. Part of that, frankly, is how you break the huddle, approach the line of scrimmage, get lined up, begin your motions — if there’s motions on that specific play. It’s a huge weapon and a huge part of our offense that we work on every day.”
Such urgency would afford Hurts more time to play chess — if the new offense still calls for it in certain situations. But Hurts acknowledged that “philosophically, things are a little different” under Mannion. The Eagles, whose passing game historically involved Hurts reading coverages and dictating pre-snap decisions, are shifting toward more “pure progression” concepts in which Hurts works through a series of predetermined routes. Andy Dalton, who is battling for the QB2 spot, said the concepts are “effective” partly because “it doesn’t matter what coverages (defenses) are playing.”
The Eagles’ old ways carried merit. Hurts was a worthy chess player with premier pieces. Wide receivers A.J. Brown and DeVonta Smith formed one of the NFL’s best duos, and Hurts proved it was worth battling the play clock to find mismatches for them — even last year. His 0.036 EPA per dropback on last-second plays in 2025 ranked 10th among starting quarterbacks. Hurts threw nine of his 25 touchdown passes with one second left on the play clock: the go-ahead, fourth-and-goal throw to Smith against the Los Angeles Rams; the 26-yarder to Brown that put the Minnesota Vikings away; the 47-yard bomb to running back Saquon Barkley that gave the Eagles an initial two-score lead against the Denver Broncos.
The reigning OPOY with a 47-yard receiving TD 🦅
DENvsPHI on CBS/Paramount+ https://t.co/HkKw7uXVnt pic.twitter.com/HKQOYnjhlp
— NFL (@NFL) October 5, 2025
But any last-second benefits in the passing game were subtracted in other phases. The Eagles’ 44 last-second runs in 2025 were significantly less efficient (-0.16 EPA per rush) than their other runs (-0.03). The Eagles also ranked fifth in the NFL with eight delay-of-game penalties, the most in coach Nick Sirianni’s tenure. Barkley’s illegal shift with two seconds left on the play clock killed a fourth-quarter comeback against the Broncos, negating Hurts’ 30-yard completion to Smith. On a pivotal third-and-7 play against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, center Cam Jurgens overshot a last-second snap over Hurts’ head. That fumble (recovered by the Eagles to end the third quarter), compounded by an illegal motion penalty the Bucs declined, staged what dysfunction looks like against a deadline.
The 2025 Eagles’ decline in the run game contributed heavily to their downfall. Unsurprisingly, linemen like Dickerson are lauding Mannion’s system for making them the aggressors . Dickerson was among the linemen in 2024 who urged Moore to adopt a run-oriented, aggressive style after their 2-2 start — an adjustment that paved the way to the franchise’s second Super Bowl championship. Barkley echoed the praise of Mannion’s offense, saying, “I feel I have a chance to be really good in this system.”
Restoring that aggression for the run game was always going to impact the passing game. And that is why the Mannion hire is the best way to view the challenge Hurts is undertaking in a high-stakes season .
Mannion’s run game is influenced by Kyle Shanahan’s and Sean McVay’s offensive principles; it involves a heavy dose of zone-blocking schemes and wide-zone concepts. It requires what Mannion has often called a “marrying” of the pass and run to make both play types look identical until the decisive moments. “Mason (Rudolph) would be the first one (who jumped
full_text:
After a disappointing first two NFL seasons, Roman Wilson has impressed so far in training camp. Gene J. Puskar / Associated Press
LATROBE, Pa. — For Mike McCarthy, the evaluation process began the moment he was hired. Film work and OTAs gave the new coach some first impressions of the roster he inherited, but it wasn’t until the players put on the pads at Saint Vincent College that the first-year Steelers coach truly got to evaluate his team.
“Mason (Rudolph) would be the first one (who jumped out),” McCarthy said. “I can’t tell you how pleased I am with him. The experience that he’s gained, I think, is incredibly valuable to us.”
McCarthy noted that Rudolph has adapted well to the footwork adjustments that have been made during QB School . The veteran backup’s arm talent has also been better than anticipated.
“You really don’t know until you stand next to them or you’re out there on the field, really how each guy throws the ball,” McCarthy said.
Rudolph’s chances of winning the QB2 job now appear stronger than when the team reported to Latrobe. As the players prepare for the first preseason game on Thursday night, let’s take a look at whose stock is up and whose is trending down.
Roman Wilson as WR3: Wilson’s career reached a crossroads after two underwhelming seasons, including last year when he was a healthy scratch. Through camp, he’s firmly in the WR3 role in three-receiver sets. McCarthy noted that Wilson’s speed gives the Steelers a threat over the top, and he’s progressed on the option routes, underneath patterns and big crossers.
“He looks to be more dynamic,” Aaron Rodgers said. “He’s making plays. He’s confident. The personality starts to come out. He’s, you know, joking around more with you in the locker room. I just love it. I love to see guys really coming into their own and really feel like they can be comfortable being their full self.”
At times last year, Wilson and Rodgers were not on the same page. There haven’t been many noticeable miscommunications this summer.
“Him and Aaron seem like they’re on the same page, their communication and where he needs to be with the concepts,” offensive coordinator Brian Angelico said. “Rome has really worked hard in his preparation and film study. I think he’s playing a little bit more quieted, mind relaxed, and just going out, playing football rather than thinking.”
Asante Samuel Jr. pushing for playing time: Joey Porter Jr.’s absence created an opportunity for Samuel to step in as a first-team cornerback opposite Jamel Dean. Spinal fusion surgery sidelined Samuel for the second half of the 2024 season and delayed his debut in 2025. After missing camp in 2025, he’s been one of the obvious standouts this summer.
“I love his ball skills, his instincts and his awareness,” McCarthy said. “I think he’s had a great offseason. I think he’s having a better training camp.”
Dean and Porter are still penciled in as the starters. However, it’s worth noting that Dean has dealt with injury problems throughout his career and has had a bit of an up-and-down camp. If the veteran corner falters or again faces an injury, Samuel has played like a starter. It will be interesting to see if they can find ways to get him on the field in sub packages or in some type of game-plan specific, matchup-oriented rotation.
Pat Freiermuth and middle-of-the-field production: Moving on from Jonnu Smith clarified a tight end depth chart that was murky at times last year. After playing a career-low 51 percent of the snaps in 2025, Freiermuth appears to be a more central piece of the offensive game plan. In particular, the tight end from Penn State has been a go-to target during the two-minute drill, especially over the middle of the field.
“I think Pat has done a really good job of controlling the middle of the field,” Angelico said. “Anytime we get a one-on-one with Pat he’s made some plays.”
Robert Tonyan’s shot at the 53: Tonyan caught 11 touchdown passes during Rodgers’ 2020 MVP season in Green Bay. Early in camp, the 32-year-old tight end, who Rodgers calls “Bobby,” has rekindled some of that old connection.
“I’m obviously partial to him, having spent a lot of time with him,” said Rodgers, who spent the team bonding trip at Kennywood riding rollercoasters with Tonyan. “I think he’s played really, really well.”
Tonyan will stick around in some way. The question is if the Steelers sneak him through to the practice squad as injury insurance for Freiermuth or if they keep him on the 53-man roster as an every-game contributor. Lately, I’m leaning toward the latter.
Derrick Harmon’s breakout year: Pretty much every media outlet predicted that Harmon would be the Steelers’ breakout player in his second NFL season. His physicality, strong hands and quick hips have been a problem for offensive linemen during one-on-one periods. He’s right on track to prove himself as a worthy first-round pick.
Payton Wilson in base: Entering training camp, it was unclear which inside linebacker would stand next to Patrick Queen in the base defense. So far, Wilson has been getting that opportunity. While his coverage ability is outstanding, block destruction is critical if he’s going to thrive on run downs. McCarthy said he’s noticed Wilson’s motor show up even more since the pads went on. He still has to prove it during the season, but he’s progressing.
Gabriel Rubio and depth in the trenches: The Athletic’s lead draft analyst Dane Brugler writes detailed scouting reports on more than 2,700 of the top draft prospects every year. Rubio was not one of them. After missing the final six games of his Notre Dame career and sliding into the sixth round, it was fair to wonder where he fit on a defensive line loaded with depth. Rubio has played mostly nose tackle and been noticeable in one-on-one situations.
“I think the biggest thing down in the trenches for all the guys when they first get in there: Do they belong? Can they jump out there in their first one-on-one, their first inside-run type situation, and so forth? Gabriel’s definitely that guy. I think he definitely belongs,” McCarthy said.
McCarthy said he can make the case for at least 10 defensive linemen making the team (between the active roster and practice squad). I’m much higher on Rubio’s chances of making the 53 than I was two weeks ago.
Robert Spears-Jennings’ roster spot: On a team with 10 draft picks, seventh rounders are far from roster locks. McCarthy noted that the backup safeties need to be special teams contributors. Spears-Jennings’ 4.3 speed and nearly 6-2 frame give him the measurable traits to thrive in this role. Because DeShon Elliott hasn’t been a full participant in team drills and Jaquan Brisker is dealing with a recent injury, Spears-Jennings has also been getting first-team reps at times. He has probably jumped up to the third or fourth safety on the depth chart.
Brandon Smith’s spot on the depth chart: When the Steelers took the field for the first day at practice, I had to check my roster when I saw No. 87 trot out with the first-team offense. Smith was not on my radar; he is now. The 27-year-old receiver overlapped with McCarthy in Dallas from 2021 to 2022 and Rodgers in New York from 2024 to 2025. Rodgers noted that Smith might have been the best playmaker during the Saturday Night Lights practice.
“When I saw him last year, he looked like he dropped about 10 pounds,” Rodgers said. “He was humongous, like just super strong and ripped, and he looks a little leaner, and I feel like he’s moving better, and really proud of him. He’s a phenomenal guy, and he’s really smart, but he’s also got some craft to his game.”
Based on practice reps, the top three receivers are DK Metcalf, Michael Pittman Jr. and Wilson. The next group has regularly featured Smith, Germie Bernard, Ben Skowronek and Max Hurleman. With Metcalf and Pittman sidelined due to injuries, it wouldn’t be surprising to see Smith get time with the first-team offense during Thursday’s preseason game.
The Steelers…

title: A playboy NFL agent was in line to run the Seahawks. Then came the crossbow killing Michael Blatt, one of the most feared agents in football, was on the verge of taking over an NFL team. Then a rival turned up dead. Katie Strang, Nathan Fenno and more
summary:
Michael Blatt was one of the most feared agents in the NFL, orchestrating holdouts and plotting a Seahawks takeover. Then a rival was ambushed with a crossbow, exposing a lethal feud fueled by money and power. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; photo: The Associated Press

full_text:
Michael Blatt was one of the most feared agents in the NFL, orchestrating holdouts and plotting a Seahawks takeover. Then a rival was ambushed with a crossbow, exposing a lethal feud fueled by money and power. Illustration: Kelsea Petersen / The Athletic; photo: The Associated Press
For this story, reporters Katie Strang, Nathan Fenno and Zak Keefer interviewed more than 70 people and reviewed more than 10,000 pages of court filings, law enforcement documents, contemporaneous accounts and other source materials.
STOCKTON, Calif. — He drove his red Mercedes along Pershing Avenue with the top down, his wavy brown hair just long enough to flap in the wind. With his monogrammed shirts and pleated pants, Michael Blatt exuded a specific 1980s California cool rooted in the certainty that, no matter what, he would never, ever lose.
Blatt chose this place to make his mark in the world. Stockton chose him, too. In the early 1980s, the San Joaquin Valley farming and port town of about 150,000 was striving to be something more, looking for heroes who measured up to their betters in San Francisco and Sacramento. Stocktonians deified the real estate developers spinning the area’s peat dirt into gold. Alex Spanos and Fritz Grupe were civic icons who raised families in town, who had their names on parks and elementary schools and arenas.
They were Stockton’s kings. Michael Blatt would become its prince.
An Army brat, Blatt said he moved 18 times before coming to the University of the Pacific to play soccer in the mid-1960s. His ambition took root. By 21, he wanted to make a million dollars. By 24, he wanted $10 million.
After graduating from UOP in 1968, he worked in finance, but Blatt would never settle for managing other people’s money. One day, legend goes, he walked into a bank and asked for a million-dollar loan. The chairman, wearing a cowboy shirt and an oversized belt buckle, said, “You’re either crazy, full of bullsh—, or you gotta be right.”
Blatt got the loan. Within six years, he had built 4,000 apartment units. Within a decade, his company tallied $120 million worth of construction. Later, he built a subdivision he called Blatt Estates with streets named after his children.
Blatt’s hazel eyes conveyed whatever he wanted someone to see in them: warmth, wisdom, cunning, menace. He lived life on the attack, chasing the next dollar, the next opponent, with inherent aggression. Once, after a dog barked at him on a walk, Blatt threatened its owner: “If your dog bites me, I’m going to own your home.”
He married Suzanne Chausse in 1968. They had two children, but she filed for divorce in 1983 amidst rumors of his infidelity, immediately becoming an adversary. Blatt dragged the legal proceedings along for three-and-a-half years, fighting for every bit of his $28 million empire. Even the parrot Suzanne once gifted him became a point of contention. She sold her fur coat to pay legal bills and petitioned the court for money to buy the children Christmas presents. At one point, Blatt told her that he could pay a man $500 “to get rid of her.” A Black man, he specified.
She got $2.2 million paid out over 15 years.
“I never did a deal I’m not proud of,” Blatt would say later.
Post-divorce, Blatt dated often and dated young. There were UOP sorority sisters he hired as secretaries and a rumored affair with the wife of a friend, a member of a prominent Stockton family. He would show up at parties or even his son’s soccer games with a striking new conquest, impressing his peers, most of whom were married.
Blatt’s father once told him he was born without peace of mind, and Stockton’s prince saw contentment as weakness. By the early ’80s, he was bored with real estate and eyeing different worlds to conquer. For years, he offered UOP football players summer jobs at his development company before counseling them on pro contracts and investments. In 1982, he co-founded the Sunwest Sports agency, which quickly amassed more than 50 NFL clients.
In an era when most agents were collegial, Blatt was ruthless. In Los Angeles, All-Pro wide receiver Henry Ellard earned the nickname “Holdout Henry” after repeated beefs with Rams management. Another client, Pittsburgh Steelers Pro Bowl linebacker Mike Merriweather, held out for an entire season to force a trade. Blatt advised Kelly Stouffer, a quarterback drafted No. 6 overall by the St. Louis Cardinals in 1987, to sit out his rookie season, telling the team’s owner that if he didn’t trade Stouffer, the quarterback would re-enter the draft the following spring. The Cardinals caved.
Blatt became one of the most feared — and loathed — agents in the NFL. He walked the sidelines before San Francisco 49ers games, chatting up players with beautiful young women at his side, the disdain wafting down from the owners’ box competing with the winds blowing off Candlestick Point. Back home, as the Stockton Record chronicled his agenting wins, Blatt became even more revered as the local businessman who outmaneuvered rich NFL owners.
Blatt had long idolized Spanos, who in 1984 bought a majority stake in the San Diego Chargers. Four years later, while negotiating Stouffer’s trade to the Seahawks, Blatt learned the Nordstrom family intended to put the team up for sale. While assembling an investment for players he represented, Blatt met California real estate magnate Ken Behring. Blatt connected Behring and the Nordstroms in the summer of 1988, facilitating the sale of the Seahawks and earning Behring’s ear and trust.
Blatt resigned as an agent, turning over his clients to a partner. He put $4.4 million in escrow to purchase a minority stake in the Seahawks. By the end of January 1989, team president and general manager Mike McCormack was out. Behring said he wanted a businessman in charge. Blatt took the initiative, planning changes to the Kingdome and mapping out the team’s targets in free agency. He told reporters he would build a dynasty.
One night, he slid into a seat at an upscale Seattle lounge. As always, there were beautiful women around, and as they drank and reveled, Blatt dropped the news:
“You’re sitting at a table with the new general manager of the Seahawks.”
Larry Carnegie punched his brakes on the freeway if someone followed too closely. He chided people for habits he avoided, like drinking coffee or taking aspirin. He once sued a friend over $150.
When he arrived in Stockton from Southern California in 1974 to attend UOP’s pharmacy school, Carnegie was 23 years old and married to a woman 12 years his senior with three children of her own. She worked as a grocery checker to help pay for his schooling, but just before graduation, he divorced her.
Carnegie saw where money was being made in Stockton. He pivoted to real estate and, in late 1981, a property manager recommended Carnegie to Blatt. By then Carnegie had a new wife, Karen, and the couple eventually took over the operation of a local firm, Riverboat Realty. Like Blatt, Carnegie could be charming. Like Blatt, he was also unencumbered by the need to be liked.
Carnegie brokered deals for Blatt and managed some of his apartments, but he was sometimes sloppy and feuded with tenants. It irked Blatt when people called Carnegie his “partner” on projects, as if they were on the same level. Perhaps it also annoyed Blatt that Carnegie, Karen and their young children moved into a home a block from Blatt’s mansion among the mature oaks of the tony Morada neighborhood.
In 1985, Blatt sold the Fremont Inn, with Carnegie brokering the deal. The buyers of the motel later claimed in a lawsuit against Blatt and Carnegie that the property’s books had been cooked. Blatt settled the suit in December 1986, but both men fumed about the financial fallout and blamed each other.
Blatt tried to wave off Carnegie like he was one of the mosquitoes that swarmed Stockton’s deltaways, but in February 1987, Carnegie scribbled a raging nine-page letter to Blatt threatening to expose damaging information if Blatt…
