full_text:
Brandon Coleman, left, and Chris Paul, center, are expected to join Sam Cosmi as starters on Washington's offensive line. Lauren Leigh Bacho / AP
ASHBURN, Va. — Brandon Coleman and Chris Paul understand the assignment.
“Born ready,” Paul said Tuesday morning.
There was one plan for the Washington Commanders’ offensive line before last Saturday, when Laremy Tunsil’s triceps muscle gave way . Now there’s a new one.
Tunsil, the five-time Pro Bowl left tackle, who was paid handsomely for his exquisite pass protection with a record-setting extension at his position, was supposed to protect Jayden Daniels’ blind side this season. But Tunsil’s injury, which will keep him out for much of the season, if not the whole year, forced a major recalibration.
Nothing’s riding on it … except, maybe, everything.
Washington will go back to the 25-year-old Coleman, the team’s third-round pick in 2024, to replace Tunsil at left tackle. Coleman started 12 games at left tackle as a rookie, but the Commanders traded essentially three draft picks to the Houston Texans in 2025 to replace him with Tunsil. Coleman was then supposed to slide in next to Tunsil at left guard, but he only lasted the first two games of last season before Paul replaced him in the starting lineup. And Paul kept the job for the rest of the season, while Coleman was a healthy scratch in some games.
Coleman, though, came to camp this year in an open competition with Paul for the starting spot. That competition is now over.
Coleman is taking over for Tunsil at left tackle. And the 27-year-old Paul, who started 15 games last season, will be next to Coleman on opening day. There doesn’t appear to be a Plan C; Washington isn’t expected to sign a veteran who could potentially step in at left tackle.
Competitors one minute, together in the trenches the next. It’s the NFL.
“Like, people always think, and it’s like, it can be true — competition can be this weird dynamic,” Coleman said Monday after practice.
“But, like, me and CP have always been really close through everything,” Coleman said. “And, even with competing, we always work together, trying to improve our game. … Even if it doesn’t work out for one of us here, we’re both good enough to play somewhere. And I have full confidence in his playing abilities, as he has in mine. You know, now it just comes to the fact where I’m playing next to him. And we can kind of play together and make this thing work.”
It’s not quite a youth movement. But if the Commanders are worse without Tunsil, and they are, they can still do some things effectively with Coleman alongside Paul.
No question: Tunsil’s absence leaves a void on and off the field. Only Denver Broncos tackle Garett Bolles, at 91, graded higher in pass protection last season than Tunsil, at 88.9, per Pro Football Focus. His ability to handle almost any elite pass rusher one-on-one gave the Commanders greater flexibility along the line to handle opposing pass rushes. Tunsil also served as a mentor for Coleman and second-year right tackle Josh Conerly Jr., hosting them last month at his annual workouts in Alabama .
But on the field — where he’ll be missed — Tunsil could get Paul straight with a quick verbal call or a physical adjustment. That allowed the duo to see things together and change the blocking scheme in real time. With a new offense to learn and the need to protect Daniels, Coleman and Paul have enough on their plates. Another significant injury — center Nick Allegretti’s calf strain on the first day of camp, which has kept him out a couple of weeks and will keep him off the field in Friday’s preseason opener against the Miami Dolphins — only adds to the stress.
“I think there’s certainly a leadership aspect that you could say is absolutely invaluable, unreplaceable, from (Tunsil’s) standpoint,” Paul said. “But we always just have a sort of next-man-up mentality. And so, that’s our challenge collectively at a unit. As we just continue on through training camp, continue on through preseason and preparing for Week 1, that’s our challenge — how we keep that continuity. And I think we’ve done a great job so far.”
Coleman started the last three games of the 2025 season at tackle, when Tunsil was out with an oblique strain. So, he and Paul have some experience playing together. Coleman played 160 snaps combined in the three games; Paul played 167. The calls and communications they worked through in those three games should help this season.
But the Commanders will need Coleman and Paul to get every rep possible together before this season, starting with Wednesday’s joint practice with the Dolphins and continuing over the three preseason games, along with an Aug. 26 joint practice with the Baltimore Ravens.
“LT had such a good way about him, even in-game to say, ‘Ok, got it. Here’s the thing,'” Dan Quinn said Tuesday. “Good news is, they do have experience starting and playing and going through it. So, they’ll have to lean on one another. I would say it’s probably similar amounts of games and starts and all that kind of stuff. But, at the end of it, it’s (them) building their time together.”
The Commanders drafted Coleman in 2024 because they thought his athletic ability at tackle could help unlock their running game. Coleman’s lateral quickness could be a good fit in the zone-blocking run attack of new offensive coordinator David Blough. Coleman was inconsistent in his pass-blocking mechanics as a rookie, but he had some solid performances, including a strong Week 3 outing in Cincinnati against then-Bengals star Trey Hendrickson.
And Paul’s two-year body transformation is striking. Last year he looked leaner and stronger; this offseason, he dropped another 20 or so pounds while appearing to lose no significant strength. While Coleman was under Tunsil’s tutelage, Paul went for a second year to OL Masterminds in Frisco, Texas, the celebrated program for offensive linemen launched in 2018 by Philadelphia Eagles tackle Lane Johnson and offensive line coach Duke Manyweather.
“Physically, I feel great,” Paul said. “I think one of the best things I love about this game is that you’re always continually looking to grow. You quite literally have to do that. And so, that comes with just how I recover. I think the team does a great job with making sure that we’re all recovered, building … certain recovery time into our schedule, that you have to do. And so I feel great.”
When Tunsil returns — whether it’s this season or next — he’ll go back to left tackle. Everyone gets that. Even if Coleman has a great season, he won’t be guaranteed a spot at tackle in 2027. We may be back at square one in a year, with Coleman and Paul again battling for a starting spot. But that’s then. This is now.
And now, Washington needs Brandon Coleman and Chris Paul to keep Daniels upright, create lanes for Jacory Croskey-Merritt and the Commanders’ running backs, and handle the weekly maelstrom of an NFL line of scrimmage, with all of its real-time set changes and decisions, without blowing a mental gasket. If I’m a defensive coordinator, I know what side of the line I’m attacking, and it isn’t the side with Cosmi and Conerly.
The kids think they’ll be all right.
“He’s a great guy to play with,” Coleman said of Paul. “One of the strongest guys I’ve played with, but also like, plays with great technique and speed, to where I’ve just got to match him, and it’s going to be a great left side.”

title: Cardinals Had a Great Training Camp — Mike LaFleur Knows There's Still Work to Do
full_text:
GLENDALE — Mike LaFleur knows what a good training camp looks like.
After spending ample time under two of the NFL's best coaches in Kyle Shanahan and Sean McVay, LaFleur's has a solid idea of what to expect walking into camp, how to navigate the dog days of summer and how to feel departing.
Yet LaFleur also knows what unsuccessful camps look like, too. His two-year stint as the New York Jets' offensive coordinator yielded forgettable results before being fired and eventually landing in Los Angeles under McVay.
The dust is now settling on LaFleur's first training camp with the Arizona Cardinals, one that was inspired by his time with the Rams. LaFleur says his four-day "block" setup of practice days was taken from McVay while other wrinkles such as utilizing instant replay during camp were also borrowed from prior stints.
What's one common denominator of a successful training camp — and did the Cardinals have one?
"They compete, and they compete the right way. It's like you got to be able to toe the line even with your brothers, and it's got to be physical," said LaFleur. "But it can't be reckless, and you got to take care of each other. So that's an ongoing process with every group I've ever been on. Even you know some of the best ones.
"That's the biggest thing. Just go out there, compete. Compete against your brothers, toe the line, play with that play style and go for it."
Whether the Cardinals had a successful training camp remains up to personal opinion. The offense and defense largely had respective ups-and-downs, though such is life during camp. Arizona emerged somewhat unscathed when it came to injuries, save for injured reserve additions such as Kaleb Proctor and Joey Blount.
It's especially difficult when LaFleur's balancing roster evaluation with installation of his first-year offense, one that admittedly has produced more promising days than negative ones. The run game has transformed and receivers are often open thanks to scheme and play-design.
"He's got a plan, and it's good to see. Not only just the offensive side of things, which obviously he's putting a lot of focus in there, but really the big picture and the whole team," said Cardinals GM Monti Ossenfort on LaFleur.
LaFleur, who admitted he was still figuring out minor details like where to stand on the sidelines while juggling attention to both sides of the ball now as a head coach, liked where his team was at overall, though there's still several strides to be made.
"They are where their feet are. They come to work every single day. They want to improve," he said when asked about what he's most pleased with.
"Again, I thought our operation was good — got a long way to go. I thought our play style was good — got a long way to go. And then they also know that we have a long way to go once that ball snapped in terms of details, fundamentals, all those kind of things within our scheme. So again, I was pleased with the work that we put in within that time, but a long way to go."
The Cardinals do have a long way to go, both physically and metaphorically. We're over a month removed from their regular season debut against the Los Angeles Chargers — which is just under 400 miles one-way.
Preparation for Week 1 is already well underway, and quite honestly it has been for awhile. The Cardinals admitted so back in June. Arizona will be far from a complete team at that point in time, though it will be a good starting point where wins and losses begin to matter.
There's plenty to be excited about regarding the Cardinals as they depart from camp with preseason battle No. 2 ensuing on Thursday. After returning from Las Vegas, they'll return to their home base in Tempe to get settled in before the regular season begins.
The offense looks promising in a multitude of ways while Arizona's defense will be tested. There's hope coordinator Nick Rallis — with a fresh but short leash after Jonathan Gannon was fired — will be able to right the ship with player health hopefully on his side.
As cliché as it sounds, only time will truly be able to tell how LaFleur's first training camp went. Arizona has a grueling regular season schedule, but excuses are like podcasts — everybody has one. The Cardinals have to be ready at SoFi Stadium on Sept. 13 and build off each performance that follows.
The heat in the desert is unique. It's not quite humid like parts in the Southeast while it reaches temperatures some along the West Coast wouldn't dream of.
While LaFleur says the team successfully kept his guys out of the scorching sun, soon he'll face a different kind of heat when records begin to matter.
"Absolutely. I think first and foremost, like we talked about, the weather and just keep these guys out of the heat," said LaFleur when asked if he accomplished what he wanted to in camp.
"We got to go battle it when we get back to Tempe, we'll be smart about that, obviously, but we are going to have to be out there at some point for obvious reasons. That was first and foremost, and like I said, we took it one day at a time, one block at a time, and I thought there was improvement, but still a long way to go."

title: How Marvin Harrison Jr. Flipped the Script After Viral Cardinals Camp Drop
full_text:
GLENDALE — The beginning of Arizona Cardinals training camp got off to a rocky start for star wideout Marvin Harrison Jr., as a string of early drops went viral for the third-year wideout.
Clips infested the internet, and it felt like everywhere you turned, you found videos or memes on Harrison.
Harrison, who had a roller-coaster start to his NFL career, is hoping to see a resurgence under new head coach and offensive play-caller Mike LaFleur .
Training camp is all about progression and improvement, and after Harrison's shaky start, LaFleur says the former No. 4 overall pick has bounced back quite nicely.
"Steady improvement," LaFleur said of Harrison's overall camp before diving into the prior drops.
"You could go very elementary, and it's like 'catch the football, never drop a ball.' Well, if you drop enough balls in this league, I don't care who you are, you're just not going to be in the league. So it's like, 'no kidding, put that away. Okay, why'd you drop it? Was it focus? What exactly was it?' All right, then you put that away, and then you really look at the process of everything. Are we creating separation? Are we coming off the ball? Like, are we in our right split? Are we are we loaded? Getting every inch of grass off the ball.
"That's one of the big things that Marv and I talk about every day. I just kind of give him one of these [leans], and what does that mean? Body lean, come off the rock, because once he gets going, he's a big dude, right? And if I'm a DB standing there, knowing I got a big dude that could run by me or can stop on a dime, that's tough.
"... Yes, he had a drop back in whatever it was, practice five, where he was wide open. Hasn't had one of those since. Great. Is he going to have probably another one at some point over his career? Yes, he is. Just like all these guys are. Then I'll flip it to the other side. What does it look like when he doesn't have the ball? What does it look like when he's getting connected? And [when] I say he, I mean all these guys. If you don't block, if you don't get sticky on DB's in this offense, you're just not going to be out there. Like, point blank period. I've been pleased with his progression and the receivers' progression in that facet of what we're trying to get done in the run game."
Harrison was open nearly as much as anybody after that point. That was never the problem, though from that moment forward, Harrison flipped a switch and made plays when called upon.
The Cardinals will need every bit of strong play possible from Harrison if they'll get things back on track. Harrison possesses all the tools needed out of a primary NFL receiving option — he's just got to go and do it.
Perhaps another year with quarterback Jacoby Brissett tossing him the ball will help.
"I think he's taken tremendous steps as far as understanding this is a long process," Brissett told reporters.
"The end result is not going to be tomorrow, and that's a battle. That's a battle for him, me, everybody on the team. The hard part is you want the results now. You want to go out there and do everything the right way, but that's why we're in the room that we're in, and and we have the opportunity to go out there and play in the National Football League because we know we can. It's just a matter of, now you got to sustain that competitive edge on a day in and day out process."
The good news? Harrison is in an advanced offense that won't solely rely on him to make plays. We've seen LaFleur consistently scheme receivers open and between the likes of Michael Wilson, Trey McBride and Jeremiyah Love among others, there's plenty of help around him.
This doesn't have to be a one-man band with Harrison — nor will it. It was encouraging to see Harrison bounce back after such a rocky start to camp.
Perhaps this is a springboard to something bigger.

title: Mike LaFleur Delivers Preseason News Cardinals Fans Have Been Waiting For
full_text:
GLENDALE — Last week, the Arizona Cardinals sat roughly 35 players who were considered starters or borderline guys.
This week, it's a different story.
The Cardinals will play their starters in Las Vegas, according to LaFleur.
"They're going to play. So we'll have our guys out there. How much? It's not going to be much. Could be one drive, max of two [drives] for those main guys. But yeah, they'll be playing, and they know that," LaFleur said ahead of the Raiders game.
Arizona's biggest veteran names that featured last week were all of Dadrion Taylor-Demerson, BJ Ojulari and Andrew Billings.
This week, the Cardinals are set to see most of their starting lineup on the field for at least a drive or two — which will see players such as Jacoby Brissett, Marvin Harrison Jr., Trey McBride, Jeremiyah Love and Budda Baker among others who weren't dressed for the Hall of Fame Game.
The Raiders are expected to play their starters this preseason, though we'll also get our first look of No. 1 overall pick Fernando Mendoza in a Las Vegas uniform on Thursday night.
"From just an actual game plan standpoint, we're not doing any of that. Like I haven't watched the snap of Vegas from last year," LaFleur said. "It's a new defensive coordinator. He was on the staff. Don't know if he's going to do the exact same or complete opposite. Have no idea."
After a big game last week, the Cardinals again will be in the national spotlight.
Today's practice puts a bow on training camp for the Cardinals, and LaFleur says the team had a successful outing in 2026:
"Absolutely. I think first and foremost, like we talked about, the weather and just keep these guys out of the heat," said LaFleur.
"We got to go battle it when we get back to Tempe, we'll be smart about that, obviously, but we are going to have to be out there at some point for obvious reasons. That was first and foremost, and like I said, I mean, we took it one day at a time, one block at a time, and I thought we there was improvement, but still a long way to go."
The Cardinals face the Raiders at Allegiant Stadium at 5:00 PM on Thursday night.
Arizona will have practiced 15 times before gathering their belongings and heading back to Tempe to finish out the preseason. The Cardinals, after this week, have preseason battles against the Dallas Cowboys and Green Bay Packers before the start of the regular season.

title: 2 Big-Name Cardinals On The Verge of Being Cut
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are one practice away from completely finishing training camp.
The team has spent weeks at State Farm Stadium in an attempt to perfect its craft, define roles and identify the best 53 players to carry into the regular season.
We've seen numerous players grow into their respective roles — while others have simply fallen out of favor.
In particular, two notable names find themselves on the verge of potentially being cut with three preseason games remaining:
Benson, a former third-round pick, clearly has potential to be a big-play running back. He's flashed that on multiple occasions through his first two seasons in Arizona.
Yet a mix of injuries and inconsistent play has put his Cardinals tenure in jeopardy as we enter the depths of the preseason. Arizona brought in Tyler Allgeier and Jeremiyah Love this offseason to take over the backfield, and with James Conner on the roster, Benson is at best battling with Bam Knight for RB4 duties.
That's a battle Knight is winning, as Benson hasn't practiced lately due to his knee injury while Knight is getting reps ahead of him. Another point to Knight's favor is his recent participation in special teams, which can make or break a player's chances of making the roster.
The conversation has now shifted from "Benson vs Knight" to "will Arizona keep Knight as a fourth running back?" ahead of cut-down day.
"Versatility comes into play there. Whether it's versatility on what they can do positionally, whether it's first and second down or third down. When it comes to special teams, that starts weighing into it," Cardinals general manager Monti Ossenfort said.
As for Benson, the possibility of either trade or release looms in the coming weeks barring an eye-opening turnaround.
Benson feels closer to actually being cut than Ojulari, though the former second-round pick very much finds himself on the ropes this preseason similar to Benson.
Injuries decimated a once exciting young career for Ojulari, who was shaping up to be a strong presence at outside linebacker before a severe knee injury knocked him out for 1.5 seasons. Ojulari's been on the bounce-back since the second half of last season, though he hasn't quite looked like the player he did coming out of LSU.
The good news for Ojulari? The Cardinals added no substantial help at outside linebacker this offseason, opting to run it back with virtually the same crew of names as before in Josh Sweat, Baron Browning, Jordan Burch, Zaven Collins and Ojulari.
However, Ojulari has struggled to separate himself during training camp, and last week's preseason outing was quite telling. In a game where the Cardinals didn't play any of their starters, Ojulari played deep into the second half against Carolina — and failed to make an impact.
"He's a fast rusher off that edge right there, and I just think it's just for him just continue to get time on task, value received. Continuing to practice," head coach Mike LaFleur said on Ojulari.
"Obviously, there's history in terms of just some of the injuries with him obviously, and just getting back out there, getting his feet underneath him, getting comfortable, using his fastball — which he has a fastball."
That fastball hasn't crossed the plate in 2026, and while Eku Leota continues to climb the Cardinals' depth chart, Ojulari is in serious danger of being off the roster.

title: Cardinals GM Monti Ossenfort Said 6 Big Things Today: Carson Beck, Josh Sweat & More
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals are nearly done with training camp.
The Cardinals wrapped up a jog-through today and are set for one last practice tomorrow before officially wrapping things up here at State Farm Stadium.
Arizona made general manager Monti Ossenfort available for reporters today — here's our biggest takeaways from what he said:
The Cardinals have all of Paris Johnson Jr., Michael Wilson and Garrett Williams eligible for massive contract extensions, though Arizona hasn't inked any of the aforementioned players just yet.
"I think the track record here the last three years is we've done extensions before the season, during the season, after the season. I think as with any negotiation/extension, those things take time, and there's a lot of conversations that go on," Ossenfort said.
"Sometimes the timelines are different, and when those match up, and when those discussions can come to agreement. I don't think there's any hard or fast rule, and I think really they come by a case-by-case basis."
Names such as Hjalte Froholdt and Dante Stills are also possible names to watch.
LaFleur, entering his first season as a head coach, has arrived prepared according to Ossenfort.
"He's got a plan, and it's good to see. Not only just the offensive side of things, which obviously he's putting a lot of focus in there, but really the big picture and the whole team," said Ossenfort.
"When you sit in that chair, a lots on your plate in terms of organization, not just the football product, but it's everything that we do. Meeting schedule, practice schedule, how we travel, everything that goes into it, and he's been he's been ready for it. He's had a plan, and it's been exciting to watch him put it in place here over the last few weeks."
Beck has been the talk of the town really since he arrived in the desert, though last week's preseason performance has plenty of buzz around the third-round pick.
So far, so good from Ossenfort's standpoint.
"I thought he got off to a good start. I think the most optimistic thing was just the clean operation," said Ossenfort.
"The way they got in and out of the huddle, the way that he handled the checks that came his way, he got the ball out of his hand, put it in the right spot. He was accurate, so [a] very positive start. A good start. It kind of builds off of what he's been doing since he got here in the spring and the early part of training camp. Obviously still got a long way to go, but thought that was a good next step in his development."
The current starter, Jacoby Brissett, is still catching up to the team's playbook after recently ending his holdout. Brissett saw a restructured deal pay him at least $15 million guaranteed for 2026.
Why did the Cardinals negotiate with a player who was already under contract through this season and clearly was not part of their plans moving forward?
"I think when we signed him, it was in a different role, and so we signed Jacoby to be a backup quarterback, and his role changed. His job changed, and the expectation changed, and so really that is what it came down to," said Ossenfort, who also added:
"With what Jacoby did last year, what he meant to the locker room — I think you guys saw just the the reaction of his teammates and how excited they were — we were excited to get the deal done with him and move forward."
Sweat's been mentioned in consistent trade buzz after the Cardinals fired Jonathan Gannon, though the team is adamant Sweat will not only be healthy for the regular season opener as he manages a knee issue — Ossenfort says the team flat-out is not interested in trading him.
"I'd say [trade] discussions that come by that, there's always a lot of talk that goes around that. We have no interest in trading Josh. We're excited to have him," he said. "Some of those discussions [we're] going to keep private. But excited to have Josh here, [he] had a great year last year. Excited for more good things out of him this year."
Love, since arriving to the desert, has been a showstopper in nearly every opportunity. He looks the part, has proved he can get open as a receiver and obviously has hit some home runs when toting the rock.
Ossenfort had a laundry list of things he liked about the No. 3 overall pick:
"Mature, professional, eager to learn, very coachable, versatile, able to do a lot of different things with him. I think coachability is a big thing. Jeremiyah was obviously a very talented player coming out [as] a high draft pick, but his improvement over the last couple weeks, just with his running style and his reads, and putting his foot in the ground and getting upfield, I think we've seen growth in that in a very short time once the pads came on," said Ossenfort.
"That's great to see out of a young player that wants to learn, wants to contribute, wants to find a role for the team, and he's been great in that respect. So excited to keep using him in multiple ways, and he's a guy that's going to help us put pressure on the defense."

title: Cardinals GM Slams Door Shut on Josh Sweat Trade Rumors
full_text:
GLENDALE — Josh Sweat has made headlines throughout the 2026 offseason, and as the team ramps up for their second preseason game, the Arizona Cardinals' top sack artist still has yet to practice.
Sweat, placed on the Physically Unable to Perform list at the beginning of camp, hasn't been spotted on the sidelines during Cardinals training camp practices as he is working through a knee injury according to head coach Mike LaFleur.
While he can't technically practice due to his placement on PUP, Sweat was also not a participant during mandatory minicamp while he wasn't present during offseason team activities, either.
Trade buzz has followed Sweat since the Cardinals fired head coach Jonathan Gannon, someone Sweat was close to. Today, when speaking with reporters, general manager Monti Ossenfort shut those talks down.
"Josh is making good progress. Josh is getting closer every day. I think Josh is going to be out there in due time to get ready for the season opener, and we're excited to get him out there and get him going," said Ossenfort.
"I'd say [trade] discussions that come by that, there's always a lot of talk that goes around that. We have no interest in trading Josh. We're excited to have him. Some of those discussions [we're] going to keep private. But excited to have Josh here, [he] had a great year last year. Excited for more good things out of him this year."
Sweat, who just turned 29, reportedly had multiple NFL teams calling the Cardinals about his availability this offseason. Yet with a thin Cardinals pass rush room, it didn't make sense for the organization to part ways with their only productive outside linebacker.
Sweat's managing a knee issue, which has mostly led to his absence throughout the bulk of the offseason and camp. The Cardinals are confident he'll be ready for the start of the regular season.
"He's in all the meetings. He's around. I know I've said it, so broken record there, but he looks really good in terms of [being] healthy, in shape, all those kind of things," LaFleur said earlier in camp.
"He's putting a lot of work in behind the scenes to make sure when he gets the green light and everyone feels good. Ultimately [we're] making sure Josh feels good both mentally and physically to go out there and perform the way [he can] because he takes a lot of pride in what his product looks like. That tape matters a lot to him as I've gotten to know him. So he's earned the right to communicate with us to say, 'hey, I feel good, I'm ready to go.'"
It will be interesting to monitor how things go for the Cardinals this season and if their trade deadline plans change at all.
It's clear there's a market for Sweat.

title: The Disrespect Toward Cardinals Star Budda Baker Has Gotten Out of Hand
full_text:
ARIZONA — Earlier this offseason, I had a nice exchange with Budda Baker on X where he essentially called me out for not believing he deserved to be listed on the NFL's Top 100 players list, where he finished at No. 75.
My shock in his placement was more so rooted in the fact that Arizona was 3-14 last season, not that Baker didn't actually deserve it. I figured Trey McBride would make the list, surely, just based on the fact that he wrapped up one of history's greatest seasons ever for a tight end. I was even surprised Josh Sweat made it at No. 78 .
I bring up the above to say... Pro Football Focus' safety rankings ahead of the 2026 season are absolutely wild.
Baker found himself at the very bottom of PFF's list at No. 32 with the following explanation:
"An eight-time Pro Bowler, Baker is a well-respected player — but one whose advanced statistics paint a more cloudy picture. Baker has sat below a 65.0 overall PFF grade in two of the past three seasons, and his coverage was especially liable last year," wrote Bradley Locker.
"Indeed, Baker’s 35.7 PFF coverage grade was the third-lowest among qualifiers, giving up a 119.6 passer rating when targeted. Also worrisome for Baker was a career-high 17% missed tackle rate. The 30-year-old is still a formidable run defender, but his coverage acumen may not project well for the close of his career."
Even the biggest haters of the Cardinals or Baker would agree that's far too low. Baker just turned 30 and still should still produce at high levels for the next few years.
Is he the best cover safety? Not quite, as Baker's game more successfully operates in blowing up run plays and closing down on ball-carriers quickly near the line of scrimmage. Still, his pure talent and freedom to roam in Nick Rallis' defense brings an unknown factor that offensive coordinators have to essentially guess on every week.
Baker, even on his worst day, doesn't belong at No. 32 in any safety rankings.
There's time for Baker to flip the script ahead of 2026, where Rallis says the star safety has looked the best he has.
"I think he looks the best he's ever looked since I've been with him, to be honest. And that's real. He'll tell you that," said Rallis.
"He's moving so good because he's just on a different level in terms of how he takes care of himself, how he trains. I think that he feels phenomenal right now, and he looks phenomenal. title: Cardinals Finally Make Larry Fitzgerald Decision Fans Have Waited For
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals are finally retiring Larry Fitzgerald's number.
After his induction into the Pro Football Hall of Fame this past weekend, the Cardinals are set to retire Fitzgerald's coveted No. 11 on Oct. 25 against the Denver Broncos.
"No one who has ever worn a Cardinals uniform is more deserving of this honor," said Michael Bidwill in a statement to the team.
"The thing I remember most about his presence here is not just how he practiced on the practice field but the way he took his profession so seriously. He is a pro's pro. His presence, both setting the tone but also welcoming people and in the locker room being a little bit of a jokester and wanting to engage everyone around him. He contributed so much to this organization and so much to this community. He means so much to us all."
Fitzgerald's gold jacket resume needs no introduction. Numerous Pro Bowls and NFL records are under his belt thanks to 17 years of high level play — all coming with Arizona.
Fitzgerald's No. 11 becomes the sixth jersey retired by the team, followed by:
For decades, Cardinals fans have loved Fitzgerald. Even after retirement, he's still one of the most popular jerseys you'll see around the desert.
During his Hall of Fame speech, he showed that same love back.
"I just want to show a little love to my Cardinal fans here in attendance today. To the Cardinal fans back home in Arizona, you guys supported us on and off the field over the years. You showed up at home games and showed up at away games, through wins and losses," he said.
"It's been 22 years and counting Arizona, and I'll spend the rest of my life trying to replenish the well of goodwill I've been lucky enough to drink from."
It was only a matter of time before Fitzgerald entered the Hall of Fame, and had his number retired. Is a statue next?
Possibly, but one step at a time. If anybody deserves the honor of having a statue outside of State Farm Stadium next to Pat Tillman, it's Fitzgerald.

title: Winners, Losers From Cardinals' Red and White Practice: Carson Beck Fires No-Look TD Pass
full_text:
GLENDALE — The Arizona Cardinals wrapped up what's likely their final open practice of 2026 with the famous Red and White scrimmage on Sunday.
Thousands of fans filled the lower bowl of State Farm Stadium as the team returned from a successful stint in Canton for Hall of Fame weekend.
The Cardinals practiced for two hours and gave fans plenty to talk about. Ranked, in no order, are our biggest winners and losers from today:
Love, who didn't suit up in Canton, got back to work and quickly reminded Cardinals fans of just how dominant he could be. Whether he was cutting up-field on runs or showing his prowess in either route-running or catching, Love's ability to win in either the pass or ground game was fully on display with the first-team offense today.
Jacoby Brissett didn't have a particularly strong or weak outing today, so it's tough to place him in either a winner or loser category. What we can say, however, is he and Harrison weren't able to connect on much of anything. Harrison was targeted five or six times with no receptions in team drills. Harrison's been able to make loads of plays in camp, though he was quiet today.
After impressing the entire football world against Carolina, Beck quickly came back down to earth again during the opening stages of Sunday's practice with some ball placement issues that were eventually paired with an interception — though he was hit while throwing. Beck responded with a dime down the right sideline in a two-minute drill followed by a no-look pass for a touchdown.
Carson Beck with a dot deep down the right sideline. Followed by a NO-LOOK pass for six. pic.twitter.com/xg8SsXBymE
That, with some work mixed with the second team, made for an overall strong day in a Cardinals quarterback room that couldn't really separate themselves.
Nolen left practice today with an unknown injury. During team activities, he appeared to be shaking his right hand before later leaving and not returning. This is the second time Nolen's left due to an injury this training camp, and his prior injury history last season again has fans anxious.
Walter Nolen just left the field with something Trainer follows him out Second time he’s left a practice with an injury pic.twitter.com/sPXRK7ntK9
Here's to hoping it was just a knock and he'll be ready to rock and roll.
The Cardinals saw all of Elijah Jones, Kitan Crawford and Eku Leota get reps with the first team today. Arizona placed safety Joey Blount on injured reserve today while Kei'Trel Clark also wasn't dressed, paving the way for Jones and Crawford to have a bit more rotation with the defense. As for Leota, he's a name to watch as he continues to rise up the depth chart in preseason play.
Allgeier told reporters one of the top things he was working on was his pass-catching ability. With Love leering behind him in the rotation, that feels like a must. So today when Allgeier saw two passes hit his hands before dropping both — one being wide open and all alone — it wasn't exactly an encouraging sign.
Robinson continues to have a strong training camp outing, winning one-on-one matchups and consistently using his raw blend of speed and power to put himself in the backfield. He had two "sacks" today (since they're not actually taking the quarterback down) and just might be preparing for that coveted leap so many want him to take.
I thought today would be a nice day to wear a navy blue polo with khaki pants. Besides looking like a grad assistant for Penn State or Navy, I was wandering the sidelines while several S.A.F.E. security folks surrounded the field (per usual doing big football events) were wearing the exact same outfit as me. I must have been confused with them four or five times, even getting some jokes from workers themselves. At least I can look the part in a potential interview if needed.

title: The 1 Thing Cardinals Want From Carson Beck After His Stunning NFL Debut
full_text:
ARIZONA — Arizona Cardinals quarterback Carson Beck impressed the entire country on Thursday night.
Beck, a third-round pick, isn't expected to start for the Cardinals with Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew currently in store, placing a heavy importance on preseason play for the rookie passer.
So far, so good, as Beck nailed his NFL debut in the Pro Football Hall of Fame Game to the tune of completing 15-of-19 passes for 188 yards and one touchdown in just over one half of play. The Cardinals were considerably impressed, according to insiders .
His performance was so good it spurred national conversations around the possibility of him starting sooner as opposed to later.
Now, the Cardinals are back home at State Farm Stadium for a short week of preparation before heading to Las Vegas on Thursday to battle the Raiders.
What's head coach Mike LaFleur looking for out of Beck?
"To continue to stack," LaFleur said.
"One day at a time. Like, let's see what we can do today. That's in the past. What do we learn from it? Because there was a lot of great learning experiences from that game in terms of stuff that us as an offense, us as a team, but each player could do a little bit better."
The Cardinals scored on their final three offensive drives of the half with Beck under center. His poise, command, ball placement and willingness to spread the ball through the three layers of defense stood out against Carolina.
However, LaFleur doesn't want to get too high or too low on Beck. He just wants consistency, and so far, that's exactly what the Cardinals have seen.
"Consistency is the truest level of performance. To go out there and do it every single day, whether it be a preseason game, a practice, all those kind of things [is important]. And so you take it for what it is in that moment," said LaFleur.
"You asked me about Carson. Carson operated the offense. We got in and out of the huddle. He wasn't rushed. Thought his eyes, his rhythm, his timing were for the most part in a good spot. And he did that for, I'd say a three and a half hour window for him. It was a two hour window, right? Because he didn't play most of that second half. Okay, learn from it, reset. Now let's get back to work, right? And that's what he's going to do, and I can say that because I know what he's made of. I liked what that was, but now we got to go do it again, not in the game but in practice."
It's unclear how much Beck will play in Vegas, though with the Cardinals leaning towards sitting their starters, the Miami/Georgia product is sure to see plenty of action again.

title: Falcons Add More OL Depth, Sign Former Eagles, Alabama OL
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons got some good injury news on Monday morning when they cleared offensive tackle Jawaan Taylor for practice and removed him from the PUP List. Taylor wasn't seen at practice yet on Tuesday morning, and the Falcons are still looking far and wide to address their offensive line depth.
On Tuesday afternoon, they put a claim on former Alabama Crimson Tide offensive lineman Jaeden Roberts, who was previously with the Philadelphia Eagles as an undrafted free agent. Roberts was placed on waivers by the Eagles, and he didn't last long before the Falcons claimed him.
Roberts was a combine invite in February. He didn't participate in any of the agility drills, but he measured a massive 6'5 1/4" and 333 pounds and did 25 reps on the bench press with 33 3/8" arms.
He was a three-year starter at Alabama and was a preseason All-American heading into 2025. He played in 10 games last season after starting 12 in 2024. He was on the Outland Trophy watch list in both 2024 and 2025, but regressed some last season with Alabama.
Roberts will compete with Kyle Hinton, Kam Dewberry, and Layden Robinson for a reserve guard spot. The Falcons took nine offensive linemen on their 53-man roster last season, and if they take nine again this year, it's likely to be Jake Matthews, Matthew Bergeron, Ryan Neuzil, Chris Lindstrom, Jawaan Taylor, Wanya Morris, Michael Jerrell, Hinton, and either Corey Levin or James Brockermeyer as the backup center.
Roberts has an uphill battle to climb to make the 53-man roster, but he could be a practice squad candidate after cuts on August 30th, when the roster must move from 90 players to 53.
The Falcons take on the Denver Broncos on Friday night in their first preseason action of 2026 under new head coach Kevin Stefanski. Roberts isn't likely to see much, if any, action with just a maximum of two days of preparation before Friday night's contest.
However, Stefanski has said he prefers starters to play in preseason games to get ready for the season. He has pegged Friday night's game against the Broncos and the preseason game three against the Miami Dolphins on August 28th as starter games. Game two next week against the Indianapolis Colts will not include many, if any, starters, as the team uses its joint practices to get first-team reps.
Roberts is just the latest player to join the Falcons this week. They've also added edge rusher Cameron Sample , running back Trey Sermon , and tight end Nick Muse as they work their way through the dog days of August to get ready for their Week 1 clash with the Pittsburgh Steelers on September 13th.

title: Will Tua Tagovailoa Play In Preseason Opener? Potential Falcons QB1 Weighs In
full_text:
Tua Tagovailoa is days away from his first opportunity to showcase himself with the keys to the Atlanta Falcons offense.
However, it remains unclear if the quarterback will play in Friday, Aug. 14’s preseason opener against the Buffalo Bills at Atlanta’s Mercedes-Benz Stadium.
“Whatever is asked of me, whatever’s asked of the guys,” Tagovailoa told reporters after practice on Tuesday, Aug. 11. “I think that’s what we’re going to go with, whatever Stefanski has.”
Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski has said in training camp that he plans to play starters in the first preseason game against the Bills and the finale against the Miami Dolphins on Aug. 28. Starters will likely rest during game two at the Indianapolis Colts on Aug. 22, with most of their reps coming in the joint practices.
Stefanski may have an answer on Wednesday, Aug. 12, on whether Tagovailoa plays in Friday’s preseason game.
“I’ll let you guys know I think, Wednesday when we talk what the plan is for the preseason games,” the head coach said. “I want to obviously sit down with the coaches and Ian and Matt, and talk through the plan, and finalize that, share it with the players, and then I’ll share it with you guys.”
Preseason could be key for Tagovailoa getting ahead in his ongoing quarterback battle with Michael Penix Jr. The former Miami Dolphin and seventh-year NFL veteran has picked up the majority of the 11-on-11 reps. Conversely, Penix takes most of the 7-on-7 plays due to not being cleared for 11-on-11 while he recovers from a left ACL tear.
There’s currently no timetable for Atlanta to name a starting quarterback.
“Preseason plays a big role for your team collectively,” Tagovailoa said. “You don’t have the coaches out there. You’ve got to go out there, make the calls, whether it’s right or wrong, you’ve got to live with them. And from there, you come in the next day, watch film, talk about it, and go from there.”
Tagovailoa has been impressive in the days leading up to the NFL preseason, following a back tightness flare-up that forced him to miss the first day of training camp .
His field vision and ability to exploit defensive breakdowns have turned heads.
“He’s getting better every day,” said Falcons quarterbacks coach Alex Van Pelt. “I think he’s getting more comfortable with the system, the play calls, and the protection adjustments. It’s tough always coming into a new system. So, picking that up, missing the first part of camp, set him back just a little bit. But the last three or four days, he’s really come on.”
The Falcons-Broncos preseason opener kicks off in Atlanta at 7 p.m. It will be televised locally on Fox 5 Atlanta, the ESPN app with an unlimited plan, or NFL+.

title: Atlanta Falcons Diving Into the Void (Years) with Latest Contracts
full_text:
With all of the changes in the Atlanta Falcons front office this past season, there was a move that went mostly unnoticed but is already having an impact. That move was the hiring of Bryce Johnston as the Senior Vice President of Football Administration/Senior Personnel Executive.
This is a big title that pretty much just means Johnston is in charge of all contract negotiations and the team's cap management strategy. Johnston has had plenty of work to do early in his tenure with the team, extending the contracts of wide receiver Drake London, running back Bijan Robinson, guard Matthew Bergeron, and tight end Kyle Pitts.
Those contract extensions included a bunch of void years, which many football fans have become used to hearing recently. But what is a void year and what does it do?
A void year is essentially “fake” years added to the end of a contract to help spread out the cap hit over more years. The signing bonus cap hit will be spread out across these void years as long as the player stays with the team he signed the contract with. Teams can add up to five void years in a contract.
This allows teams to be more flexible with their cap space now at the risk of it coming back to bite them in the future if the player decides to leave. A new contract or extension can include some of the money that was pushed into void years to avoid the balance coming due all at once.
This void year strategy has gained popularity recently and was heavily used by Johnston's former employer, the Philadelphia Eagles, where he served as a cap space strategist.
The strategy works well at creating some extra cap space and doesn’t really have any drawbacks as long as the players re-sign with the team and your owner has a lot of cash on hand to give out large signing bonuses.
So how did Johnston apply this void year strategy to the Falcons' recent contract extensions?
To start, there are four void years applied to Pitts' extension, and five applied to London, Robinson, and Bergeron’s deals. In total, that is 19 void years for signing bonuses to be extended over.
The result is over $10 million in cap savings for this year, despite handing out massive extensions. The team has the flexibility to use on plugging holes that are bound to pop up as the season progresses, including a possible edge replacement following the Jalon Walker injury. The Falcons can also carry the savings into next season.
The collateral is a possible $115 million dead cap hit if none of them resign with the team when their extensions run out. That is why these extensions and void years in particular point to an obvious point the front office is making: invest in young talent. Bergeron is the oldest of the quartet at just 26 years old.
Matt Ryan, Ian Cunningham, and Johnston believe that the Falcons have a strong young core on the offensive side of the ball and want to keep these players around for years to come despite the risk that comes with it.
Void years, contract extensions, and cap space are all very confusing and are handled by people much smarter than me, but hopefully this story gave some insight into the Falcons' extensions and cap space strategy.

title: Falcons Making Moves, Sign former Minnesota Vikings Tight End
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons have been busy this week making roster moves as they fine-tune their 90-man training camp roster ahead of their clash on Friday night with the Denver Broncos.
On Monday, they announced they had activated offensive lineman Jawaan Taylor and signed edge rusher Cameron Sample and running back Trey Sermon.
They announced another move on Tuesday morning with the signing of former Minnesota Vikings tight end Nick Muse. In a pair of corresponding moves, they waived undrafted free agent wide receiver Le'Meke Brockington and linebacker Malik Verdon.
Muse was originally a seventh-round selection by the Vikings in the 2022 NFL Draft from the South Carolina Gamecocks. Muse spent three years in Columbia and had his best season in 2020 with 30 catches for 425 yards and a touchdown.
He played 16 games with the Vikings in three years, mostly on special teams. He had one catch for 22 yards in 2023.
He's spent the last year playing the roster shuffle on several teams' practice squads, including the New York Jets, Detroit Lions, and LA Rams.
New head coach Kevin Stefanski has expressed interest in playing some three-tight-end sets on offense, and Atlanta has three tight ends that appear to be locks to make the roster in Kyle Pitts Sr., Austin Hooper, and Charlie Woerner. Joshua Simon and Jack Velling are the only other tight ends at training camp, and neither of them appears to definitively warrant a spot on the 53.
More likely, the Falcons could keep two tight ends on the practice squad and take turns using game-day elevations if they want to add a fourth tight end for games.
Brockington was signed by the Falcons as an undrafted free agent, but he wasn't able to separate himself from the crowd to try and make the Falcons' roster as a fifth or sixth receiver, if they decide to keep six.
Drake London, Jahan Dotson, Olamide Zaccheaus, and Zachariah Branch are all but locks to make the team. Chris Blair has been the best receiver outside of that quartet, and his special teams contributions may help determine if he can beat out Dylan Drummond and/or Cash Jones for a 5th spot. Jones looks like he could be the guy if the Falcons keep six. He has versatility to play slot receiver, running back, and help special teams.
The new-look Falcons play on Friday night in their first preseason action against the Denver Broncos. Roster cutdowns happen on August 30th, and players like Muse, Simon, and Velling are all on the bubble to make the initial 53.

title: Falcons Fans Get Brutal Suspension Rumor on James Pearce Jr.
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are bracing for a decision from the league office on the immediate future of James Pearce Jr., and Josh Kendall of The Athletic believes that it could be far more significant than some fans think.
The team has not heard anything from the NFL, but there is a reasonable expectation that word could come down before rosters trim down at the end of the month. Guesses from most around the organization have hovered around six games, but Kendall thinks that number could grow as high as eight, or half the regular season.
ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler seems to agree with Kendall’s sentiment, saying there is still “uncertainty” regarding the 2026 position and that how the team deals with the edge position is “worth watching” this summer. One such update came earlier Monday, with the Falcons signing Cameron Sample and moving DeAngelo Malone to the reserve/PUP list.
With Pearce’s unknown situation and the training camp injury to Jalon Walker that will cost him the season, the position remains in a worrying state. Both players saw late-season surges in 2025 that put them atop the rookie sack leaderboard, and both were expected to build on that success in 2026.
Now, the Falcons are left scrambling for answers.
The early returns from the summer appear to indicate that the Falcons do not expect to have Pearce in the early portions of the year. He rotated in with the starters on Saturday but has largely worked with the reserve units.
That could also have something to do with his absence for most of the team’s offseason program, but time will tell.
“He's doing a nice job, and I appreciate the work that he's putting into it,” Stefanski said Monday about continuing to work Pearce into the rotation. “We'll continue to roll guys in at all positions. We've had a lot of injuries now at the edge in particular. We're going to ask everybody to do a little bit more, but he's continuing to do everything we're asking him to do.”
As it has since Pearce was first arrested in February, this story will continue to evolve . In the meantime, the Falcons will continue preparing for Friday night’s preseason game with the Denver Broncos. Kickoff for that game is set for 7:00.

title: Atlanta Falcons Bolster Running Back Room With Veteran Signing
full_text:
Before the Atlanta Falcons begin their preseason this Friday at home, the franchise has made a late addition to their running back room on Monday evening.
Atlanta added sixth-year tailback Trey Sermon to its roster, most recently coming from the Pittsburgh Steelers for only one season. Sermon will look to make a name for himself on his fifth team since being drafted in 2021.
The report was announced by the franchise’s senior reporter, Tori McElhaney, to begin the week.
Falcons signed veteran free-agent running back Trey Sermon.
Atlanta’s offense gains a piece who returns to his home state of Georgia while looking to bring back the player of old from his college days. Selected in the third round by the San Francisco 49ers, Sermon wasn’t able to create a role while battling injuries that led to his exit.
After the 2021 season, the running back bounced around to the Philadelphia Eagles, Indianapolis Colts and Pittsburgh Steelers, most recently playing for the latter despite not finishing with any statistics.
Sermon was a highly touted prospect coming out of Ohio State in his senior season, seeing time at Oklahoma from 2019-20. From his time as a Buckeye, he ended up bursting onto the scene with a 331-yard rushing performance in the 2020 Big 10 Championship, the most in an FBS championship and the program’s history.
He returns to the Peach State, joining a running back room that will be obviously headlined by third-year star Bijan Robinson. With the departure of Tyler Allgeier to the Arizona Cardinals, the spot to complement Robinson is up for grabs, and Sermon will look to take advantage of that with preseason reps.
Atlanta added Brian Robinson Jr. to help aid the effort, with Tyler Goodson, Nathan Carter and Cash Jones adding value behind them in the running backs room. Sermon will look to slot himself into the 53-man roster that will be cut at the end of the summer.
Sermon recorded 134 carries for 505 yards and three rushing touchdowns in his five seasons in the NFL, also having 138 receiving yards and a touchdown through the air. He’s started in five games across his 46 contests of his professional career.
Over the next four weeks, the journeyman will look to stand out throughout the Falcons’ four-game preseason slate that kicks off at Mercedes-Benz Stadium this weekend. While both Robinsons will bring the most production on the ground next season, another solid tailback would only help Atlanta’s offense during the year.
The Falcons kick off against Denver at 7 p.m. on Friday, and the game will be broadcast on ESPN Unlimited.

title: Falcons Get Injury Boost Ahead of Preseason Clash with Broncos
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons , like most teams around the NFL this time of year, have already dealt with their share of injuries as they get ready for Week 1's opening game against the Pittsburgh Steelers.
However, on Monday afternoon, the team got a boost with the return of right tackle Jawaan Taylor, who was cleared to join practice for the first time as a Falcon. He was removed from the active/PUP list and should join the team on Tuesday morning.
Taylor was signed as a free agent shortly after long-time starter Kaleb McGary announced his retirement. McGary suffered a knee injury last year and decided to call it a career this season rather than further risk his knee.
Taylor signed for $5 million, but according to Spotrac, that didn't include any guaranteed money. As each day ticked by with him on the outside looking in, it looked like a possibility that he might not play for the Falcons at all.
Those concerns were alleviated with the news and still having four-plus weeks to get ready for the regular season against the Steelers. The Falcons take on the Denver Broncos on Sunday night at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, but it's highly unlikely that Taylor will see action.
"He obviously hasn't been in there yet, but has been extremely dialed in in meetings as he gets his body ready," head coach Kevin Stefanski said on Monday morning. "So I'm very confident in how he's prepared to date, and now with this next step of coming off the list where he can do a little bit more, can get in uniform, can go join the team, I think you'll see him continue to make strides."
He'll need a bit of an acclimation period before going full speed; the rest of the team has already been at training camp for two weeks, after participating in OTAs and minicamp in June.
In his place, Michael Jerrell has seen the bulk of the action with the No. 1 unit next to All-Pro Chris Lindstrom. Taylor joined the Falcons after spending the last three seasons with the Kansas City Chiefs.
Taylor was originally a second-round pick by the Jacksonville Jaguars in the 2019 NFL Draft. He spent four years with the Jaguars, and he started every game the Jaguars played in those four years.
He signed a big-money free agent contract with the Kansas City Chiefs before the 2023 season. He started 17 games in 2023 and 16 games in 2024. He split time last year, playing in 12 games with all of them starts.
The Chiefs released him in a cap-saving move before he was scooped up by the Falcons.
The book on Taylor is that he's a bit of the opposite of McGary. While McGary was an excellent run blocker, he struggled in pass protection. Taylor is better in pass pro, but not as good a run blocker. The pass protection aspect of his game probably appeals more to Falcons management, as they don't need to have the best run blockers to spring Bijan Robinson.
Taylor must also clean up his penalties . He was flagged 14 times in 2024, his last full season as a starter, and had 10 penalties in 12 games last season.
The Falcons will be glad to have him back at practice this week. He brings much-needed experience and talent to a position that has Michael Jerrell, Ethan Oniawna, and Brandon Walton sharing snaps. That trio of players has a combined five NFL starts among them.

title: Atlanta Falcons Sign Former Cincinnati Bengals Edge Rusher, Per Report
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH, GA - The Atlanta Falcons began the season with one of the more interesting group of edge rushers in the NFL. However, they lost Jalon Walker to injury last week and quietly moved DeAngelo Malone to the reserve/PUP list.
With the status of James Pearce Jr. still unknown for the season opener on September 13th against the Pittsburgh Steelers, the Falcons suddenly find themselves very thin at edge.
They've helped remedy the situation by signing former Cincinnati Bengals fourth-round pick Cameron Sample, according to a report from CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz .
Sample was taken with the No. 111 pick in the 2021 NFL Draft and is a native of Snellville, Ga., where he attended Shiloh High School. He attended Tulane for four seasons and had 10.5 sacks. His best season came as a senior in 2020, when he had 52 tackles, 7.5 tackles for loss, and 5.0 sacks.
There wasn't an NFL Combine when Sample was coming out of Tulane, but he measured just a tick under 6'3 and 270 pounds at his pro day and added an impressive 37-inch vertical leap.
Sample was a regular in the Bengals' rotation at edge rusher during his first three seasons. He played in 14 games as a rookie, 16 in his second season, and all 17 in 2023, including one start. He was placed on injured reserve in August of 2024 after an Achilles injury and didn't play a down.
He returned to action in 2025 and played in 14 games with 2 starts. He tied his career high last season in sacks with two after coming back from missing all of 2024.
In four active seasons with the Bengals, he played 61 games with five starts, had 85 tackles, 8.0 tackles for loss, and 7.0 sacks.
Sample joins the Falcons' Samson Ebukam, who joined the team as a free agent in March, as a player who lost all of 2024 to an Achilles tendon injury. Sample relied more on size and strength in his role as an edge setter and was able to return to his normal production a little sooner than Ebukam.
Ebukam comes in roughly 25 pounds lighter and had 9.5 sacks in 17 games with the Colts before missing all of 2024 with a similar injury. Ebukam had just two sacks in 2025 as he worked to regain his full agility and burst last season.
He says he's fully healthy this season and notices a clear difference in his explosiveness at Falcons training camp.
Ebukam has been impressive in training camp and looks to have one of the starting edge roles locked down for the Falcons. Pearce's status is still unclear, but he has a spot as a pass rusher when he's fully cleared. Azeez Ojulari and a resurgent Bralen Trice look good for a spot on the 53-man roster along with defensive end Cam Thomas, who plays a standup edge in the Falcons' big packages.
There's an opportunity for Sample to make this team. He has a similar skill set to Trice and Thomas, so a lot will depend on how many big edge rushers the Falcons want to keep on cutdown day on August 30th.
Sample should get acclimated to the team this week and may see some time on Friday night when the Falcons take on the Denver Broncos in their first preseason game of 2026.

title: Falcons Are Doing Something Different at Training Camp Under Kevin Stefanski
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons are ushering in a new generation this season, and training camp has given the latest example of the ‘new’ up at team headquarters.
Pads came on for the first time last week, but those weren’t the only thing that popped. For the first time that this writer can remember, the players were tackling and bringing each other to the ground during team drills.
First-year Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski introduced these periods into Wednesday and Friday’s practices. He has regularly been a proponent of working live tackling into camps, going back to his days as an assistant under Andy Reid with the Philadelphia Eagles and watching stars Brian Dawkins and Brian Westbrook go at it.
"We will always do what's safe for our players, and we will never do anything that's unsafe," Stefanski said about his methods. "I think there's a way to work hard, and I think there's a way to work smart. I think there's a way to practice live because that's what the game is, and I think there's a way to do it safely. I think you saw that the other day, and we'll continue to do that throughout this camp."
For the players, some have experienced training camps like this, and others have not. Newcomer Tyler Goodson is among those who have been part of them, and he appreciates that Stefanski has instituted the practice with the franchise.
"It’s good," the running back said in support of the hitting during practice. "It’s a good way to get the guys their fundamentals and their technique right coming into preseason and going into Week 1."
It had been a while for cornerback Mike Hughes, but he thinks the live tackling has helped grease up the pads and set the tone for a physical team.
"Obviously, we want to be hitting a different color," Hughes explained. "But it starts at practice, and it’s been good for us… There has to be a way to break in the pads and to get that feel back because there’s no other way to simulate that."
Players like Drake London, on the other hand, have never experienced something like this during their professional careers, but agreed that it helps with the acclimation – both mentally and physically.
"We’re callusing our bodies up to go in and play an actual game," the star wideout said. "It’s really good for us. It was a cool thing that coach implemented, and I’m excited we’re doing it."
The practices have been physical, but all of them have a purpose and an expectation that the hitting brings out the competitive fire this team will need come September.
"I think the guys understand how to do that the right way. You're still not taking a shot, quote-unquote, on one of your teammates. You wouldn't take a cheap shot type of thing," Stefanski finished. "But like I've said before: to get ready to play football, you have to play football."

title: Falcons Have Several Options to Solve Their Biggest Secondary Question
full_text:
FLOWERY BRANCH – The Atlanta Falcons spent much of the offseason rebuilding one specific area of their secondary: the nickel.
Billy Bowman Jr. quickly locked down the position during training camp last summer, and then showed some real promise early in his rookie season, but a torn Achilles cost him the chance to finish his first year strong and perhaps the early parts of his second. In his place, the Falcons were fortunate to have a resurgent Dee Alford in the mix. The veteran had a career season after Bowman went down, but he was lost during free agency .
The loss of both players left an obvious hole for the Falcons to replace. In 2026, the scheme remains the same, but the faces will be new.
“Everybody’s working,” cornerback Mike Hughes said about the secondary as a whole, and bringing the new players along during camp. “Nobody’s afraid of the competition. Everybody’s coming along well, and I just think it [the new competition] makes everybody better at the end of the day.”
As a unit, the secondary was strong for the majority of the season. They finished No. 13 in yards allowed (200.4), No. 14 in EPA per pass allowed (-0.08), and didn’t allow a single 200-yard performance until Week 8. It was only after injuries to Bowman and Hughes that the unit slowed down, allowing 230 or more passing yards in six of their final eight games.
But with Bowman continuing his long rehabilitation process and Alford no longer being an option, Ian Cunningham made a pointed effort to infuse the room with new heads that can wear a variety of hats.
Chief among those new players are rookie Avieon Terrell, who can shift between the inside and outside cornerback positions, and safety Sydney Brown, who is built strikingly similar to Bowman and can flip between his listed position and being a heavy nickel corner.
“You have to be okay with mixing and matching in this day and age,” Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski said. “The idea that you just have 11 guys that play just is not realistic. I feel very, very fortunate to have guys at the nickel position, multiple guys at the nickel position that can do different jobs.”
With defensive coordinator Jeff Ulbrich emphasizing multiplicity in his fronts, having a nickel who can play both coverage and support the run gives Atlanta more flexibility with its pre-snap looks. Their ability to play multiple spots could allow Atlanta to move them around based on personnel, rather than locking them into traditional nickel roles.
Of the other options, A.J. Woods is the lone healthy returning option for the Falcons inside, and he has received plenty of starting reps through the first week of action. Veteran Darnay Holmes is another option for Ulbrich to toy around with, and he has already made it clear that he has high expectations for himself this season.
Those two, along with Terrell, are the primary candidates to start for the Falcons early in the season, while Brown could be involved in goal-line or run-support situations. The rotation will continue to evolve as the summer goes on, but most importantly, the Falcons have clearly given themselves more options to play with.
“Being around these guys, there’s a lot of development going on,” Holmes said. “I’m just excited for the room to grow and cultivate.”
All four have a path to the job. That flexibility, more than any single player winning the role outright, may be exactly what the Falcons were looking for.

title: Durham Smythe Is The Only Raven Who Has Worked With Their Rookie Offensive Coordinator. He's A Big Fan
full_text:
One of the more fascinating aspects of the Ravens hiring a then-29-year-old who had never called a play to run their new offense is the fact he also isn’t seeing many familiar faces on the roster or coaching staff.
There is nary an assistant coach or a player on the roster with serious ties to Declan Doyle or his primary mentor, Broncos coach Sean Payton. In a situation like this, with so much new and so much new for Doyle, you’d think there might be more coaches on the staff with deep ties to Payton (Joe Lomardi is one of them). And if not key veterans who were with Doyle in Chicago last season, then several who at least were stalwarts at some point for Payton (who Doyle was with in New Orleans and Denver).
Just blocking tight end Durham Smythe, who will likely prove to be a sage signing and real factor in a multiple and diverse run game that will be under center more than we’ve ever seen during quarterback Lamar Jackson’s tenure here . We believe Smythe has plenty to offer in that regard and is a great value (think of a mauler in the vein of Nick Boyle).
But we’re not talking someone who is going to be on the field all the time and not exactly playing a position where his mastery of Doyle’s nascent scheme if going to be readily amplified Heck, most of the tight end room is compromised of guys who even the Ravens aren’t sure can play in the league yet .
This isn’t like a center or a No. 1 wide receiver. Regardless, based on one year with the Bears in which Doyle wasn’t even really the offensive coordinator (he didn’t call plays), Smythe is the resident Doyle expert for now.
“He’s built for this,” Smythe said of Doyle after Tuesday’s practice. “Obviously, he's risen pretty quickly in this field, but it's deserving. You could see that last year — obviously [Chicago Bears head coach] Ben [Johnson] is calling the plays, but Declan is right there knowing what to do.
“He could have called plays if he needed to. He's built for this. He's been around some great offensive minds in the last decade, and now he's kind of making all of those his own thing. It's pretty exciting, and I'm excited to work with him."
Doyle is bringing quite a bit of what Payton believes in most , as the Broncos coach explained to us in depth on “The Daily Flock Show” last month. He will take early-down deep shots out of play action, believes deeply in selling play action under center and operating the quarterback in those traditional five-and-seven-step drops, with “Joker” body types toggling between positions.
Smythe is an old-school impact player at the line of scrimmage and won’t be targeted much. But with Doyle asking so many players to try to operate from multiple positions during this install, his depth of understanding about those concepts is invaluable; again, it’s surprising there aren’t a few more like him sprinkled across various position groups.
"I think the way this offense is taught,” Smythe said, “whether it be last year in Chicago or this year here — you kind of want to stress the players as much as possible, as fast as possible. So, at the beginning of teaching things, it can be a little rough because there's so much information thrown at you at once.
“But, I think over the longevity of the season — which you kind of saw with us last year in Chicago — we started a little slow and then everything caught on at once. Obviously, we're in a race to master it faster than that … There's a lot to work on in that regard, but we're definitely in a race over the next three weeks."
Smythe could be a resource for the offensive linemen, too, with pre-snap penalties and out-of-sync linemen a major issue with the Bears last season into about the midpoint of the season. That’s something Doyle wants to avoid if possible. Easier said than done and especially with the backups playing so much in the upcoming preseason games, the flags are going to fly.
Perhaps during the flurry of roster transactions that come around final roster cuts to 53 more players with past ties to the system will show up on the roster. For now, Smythe pretty much stands alone

title: Early Reports Indicate Ravens May Have Avoided Major Injury With Top CB Nate Wiggins
full_text:
There is no definitive timetable yet for Ravens cornerback Nate Wiggins after he went down in practice Tuesday and had to be carted off the field. Head coach Jesse Minter said after practice that he is “optimistic” about the outcome and reports from The Athletic and NFL Network are indicating that will be the case.
While there are still no details on the extent of the injury, an MRI was conducted and Wiggins avoided any real structural damage , according to those reports. Of course, a scenario such as that still doesn’t necessarily mean that Wiggins won’t miss several weeks or more. Minter, also the defensive playcaller, was very nebulous about injury inquiries in general in the offseason, and in his first instance as a head coach, it remains to be seen how directly he will asses these situations.
Wiggins suffered the still-undisclosed injury after tangling with rookie receiver Ja’Kobi Lane. The fact he was carted off, the import of this player and the fact we are still in early August would all point to at least some time on the shelf for Wiggins, who carries a slight frame. Wiggins was already not going to play in Saturday’s pre-season game as one of the team’s key players.
“One of those plays, really not much between those guys,” Minter said of the collision that ended Wiggins’s practice.  “I think there is optimism, but, again, we’ll look at it and see where it’s at.”
Wiggins’s departure came at a time when the Ravens defense was getting quite healthy. Defensive linemen John Jenkins and Travis Jones recently returned from the PUP list and Minter said on Tuesday that he believes young linebacker Teddye Buchanan, returning from surgery, could perhaps do the same in the coming weeks.
With Marlon Humphrey coming off a poor 2025 season and off to a rough start in camp – the $19M corner noted Minter rightfully referred to his play as “trash’ this summer –the Ravens need Wiggins to make plays on the ball and continue his ascent. Staying healthy is a big part of that.
Minter lives in nickel and dime coverages loaded with defensive backs and plays as much quarters coverage as anyone in the NFL, something that should help Wiggins flourish. Humphrey is best suited for the slot, and the boundary corner situation gets very murky all of a sudden without Wiggins.
