title: Jesse Minter Confident in Ravens’ Cornerback Depth After Nate Wiggins Injury
full_text:
Just when it seemed like the Baltimore Ravens dodged their first significant injury scare to a prominent starting player, with two-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers missing just one practice after suffering a quad contusion on Saturday, they got hit with another on Tuesday when starting cornerback Nate Wiggins was carted off the field about an hour into practice.
According to multiple reports from reporters in attendance, the third-year pro went down with what looked like a left knee/leg injury while covering rookie wide receiver Ja'Kobi Lane and was in noticeable pain. He couldn't put any weight on his injured leg and was helped off the field by trainers.
" He got his feet tangled with Lane while covering a go route and fell hard to the ground," ESPN's Jamison Hensley accounted . "Trainers looked at the left leg and knee of Wiggins, who was in visible pain. He is the first player to be carted off in this year’s training camp."
Head coach Jesse Minter addressed the unfortunate development in his opening statement when speaking with the media during his post-practice press conference. While he didn't have any updates to give or declarative statements about Wiggins' injury, as the former first-rounder will need to undergo further testing to determine the severity of it, he did express hope that it might not be anything long-term.
“I don’t have a ton of information on that yet. We'll kind of get it looked at, see where it's at," Minter said. “I think there’s optimism.”
Wiggins has been on an ascent since he finished strong in the second half of his rookie season in 2024. The former first-round pick established himself as the Ravens' top cornerback last year, leading the team with a career-high 14 pass breakups and finishing second in interceptions with three. Heading into the 2026 season, he is slated to be a central figure in Minter's coverage plan for the overall secondary and is projected to break out in a good way.
Without him, they might have to rely more on a zone-heavy approach instead of using as much man-coverage that someone of Wiggins' ability would've allowed them to deploy more regularly.
"Obviously, Nate is an elite player," Minter said. "I think Nate has [the] potential to be one of the top corners in the whole league."
While losing Wiggins for any amount of time would be a tough blow for a Baltimore defense looking to rebound from what was a widely inconsistent and overall abysmal 2025 campaign, the team's cupboard at the position is far from bare.
They still have a pair of 10th-year veterans in four-time Pro Bowler Marlon Humphrey and Chido Awuzie, who were slated to play prominent roles even before Wiggins went down and have been performing well in training camp as of late, further inspiring more belief in the coaching staff that they are still well-equipped at cornerback.
"I got a lot of confidence in the corner room," Minter said. "I look at Marlon, [and] he's probably had his best couple days that last couple times out here. Chido, this guy has played a ton of football and played at a really high level. I think he's had a great camp up to this point.
The Ravens also have a handful of young talent that they're really excited about and have also been putting together strong showings in camp thus far in third-year pro T.J. Tampa, second-year pro Keyon Martin and fifth-round rookie Chandler Rivers.
"T.J. Tampa has done a lot of great things; Keyon Martin has done a lot of good stuff, Chandler [Rivers] has done a lot of good stuff and we got some young guys battling for trust and spots so I feel really good about the secondary overall."
The aforementioned other "young guys" include second-year pros Bilhal Kone and Robert Longerbeam, who were 2025 sixth-round picks, and Marquise Robinson, who was an undrafted free agent last year. Wiggins' injury won't impact the approach that the coaches already take with the other players at the position because they are always preparing them for bigger roles if and when their numbers are called.
"I don't think you're ever not rushing guys to go play; we're doing everything we can to get T.J. Tampa ready to play, to get the young guys ready to play," Minter said. "I don't think [Wiggins' injury] changes that. It might change the amount of reps they get against a certain group and the opportunities they get in practice but again, I like where that room is at."

title: The Ravens TE Room Is Underwhelming. Even The Coaches Can't Really Spin It Otherwise
full_text:
The Ravens are short on tight ends.
Perhaps, woefully short on tight ends.
They are at least a Darren Waller short at tight end , and probably more than just a Darren Waller short. July and August are the time in the NFL calendar centered around hype and false hope. It’s when all the key veterans are undoubtedly in “the best shape of their lives” and youngsters are “about to make the leap” and in a Ravens camp with no shortage of all of the above narratives in abundant supply across their roster, not a peep about the promise or progress of any of their tight ends. Veteran or newbie.
Now, it’s still early of course. Okay, not for Mark Andrews, who looked cooked last year and whose contract extension – the timing of which was more to rub it in the face of ongoing tight end Isaiah Likely that an actual reward for anything trending in the right direction with Andrews – will be a massive mistake . And he isn’t explosive and he has no twitch and he can’t even run like he used to or jump like he used to at a position where those are carrying traits now more than ever.
And no one has been overtly impressed with the two project tight ends they drafted because they are project tight end and late-round picks with huge holes in their game as it pertains to the NFL. We had general managers and scouts we fully trust break them down for us in the spring, and we aren’t expecting much from either this season . Plenty of time for them prove everyone wrong, but even Ravens tight ends coach Zack Grossi made it clear where rookies Matthew Hibner (133rd overall) and Josh Cuevas (173rd overall) stand after Tuesday’s practice.
“Pleased with the way those guys have approached things so far, but we’ve got a long way to go,” Grossi said, in what could go down as quite the understatement.
I believe this is the worst position group on the roster, and it’s not particularly close. Long-term, maybe they have a diamond in the rough or two for down the road, but short term they need impact options at this position if Andrews is what I think he is. And they simply doesn’t exist. And general manager Eric DeCosta better to ready to step in and fix it, because the wide receiver room aint brimming with proven NFL difference-makers, either.
Good on the Ravens for landing a legit blocking tight end in Durham Smythe in free agency, who knows the system from being under Ravens coordinator Declan Doyle in Chicago – HYPER. But that ain’t gonna do much for two-time MVP quarterback Lamar Jackson in trying to unlock deep options in a brand new offense being installed by a 30-year-old coordinator calling plays for the first time.
As for how far this group needs to go, they haven’t been shining even in drills that are designed by their very nature to showcase them. They aren’t flashing. As Grossi explained it, a lot of what Hibner and Cuevas are being asked to do in the full panorama of NFL tight end duties is “very foreign to them” and vastly different from anything they were asked to do in college.
That’s the reality. This is projection and guesswork in spades with this group. The Ravens passed on grabbing more polished top college tight ends to grab developmental edge Zion Young in the second round, and that gamble could have major ramifications on how this season plays out.
“We’re throwing a lot at them,” Grossi noted, “and they’re doing a good job of just working, just keeping their head down and not getting too worried with the results right now.”
Cuevas said: “They’re giving us a lot of stuff really quicky. And going from that college offense to an NFL offense, it can get pretty overwhelming.”
Gulp. An understandable gulp. But gulp.
Holding up in the trenches in the NFL – even if just engaging a block for an instant before releasing – is a whole new world for these two. Grossi said he is “pleased with how they are attacking it,” but just basic footwork and hand placement – as rudimentary as it gets – is part of their learning curve.
“Look, you have to be able to block in this league as a tight end,” Grossi said. “You have to be able to win the C Gap - all the different places we put tight ends. We put them on the ball and off the ball. We do two-back runs.
“We line them up at receiver. We do perimeter schemes … zone schemes and gap schemes. So, you have to be versatile, and you have to be able to handle different blocks.”
Color me concerned about every individual in this room, save for Smythe, as well as the total construct of it. There isn't one metric with Andrews that isn't in steep decline and he's never scored a postseason touchdown and comes up most small when it matters most . Losing Likely and Charlie Kolar in free agency is a big deal.
“The room is built around Mark, and everybody compliments him,” as Grossi explained it.
That’s precisely the problem.

title: Ravens Holding Their Breath As Top Corner Nate Wiggins Carted Off From Practice
full_text:
Of all the young players on the Ravens roster, few are carrying higher immediate expectations than top corner Nate Wiggins. And he provided the first major injury scare of Jesse Minter’s first training camp as a head coach on Tuesday.
Wiggins tangled with rookie receiver Ja’Kobi Lane in a one-on-one drill and had to be carted off the field with what for now is an undisclosed injury. Anytime a player of this stature is unable to finish a camp practice it’s a big deal, and leaving on a cart is never a great sign, either.
Minter, who took over for John Harbaugh after a nearly 20 year run as head coach in Baltimore, offered few details after practice as the Ravens medical team gathers more information about the extent of the injury. Wiggins was already not going to play in Saturday’s preseason game as one of the team’s key players.
Minter agreed there “was not a whole lot there” in the interaction with Lane, though Wiggins did fall to the ground. “One of those plays,  really not much between those guys,” as the coach explained it.
“I think there is optimism,” Minter said, “but, again, we’ll look at it and see where it’s at.”
The setback, if significant, comes at a time when the Ravens just activated defensive tackle Travis Jones from the Physically Unable to Perform list, getting the defense back to full health save for a few young players still coming back from surgery (most notable linebacker Teddye Buchanan).
Wiggins, a first round pick two years ago, has a rough second half to the season, but nearly as rough as veteran Marlon Humphrey, who was one of the most successfully picked on starting corners in the NFL. Humphrey has had a rough go of it so far this summer, saying the staff rightfully called his play “trash” at times, and we suspect he was likely headed to the slot more fulltime.
Veteran Chidobe Awuzie was brought back on a less free agent deal after a great 2025 season – one of few standouts on one of the worst defenses in the NFL – but injuries have been an issue for his as well and keeping him on a pitch count makes sense. The Ravens have some young corners dealing with injuries as well.
The expectation is Wiggins will get his hands on the football more in this zone-based scheme, with Minter’s defenses with the Chargers top three in interception rate the last two seasons . Wiggins is sticky in coverage but all the defensive backs were exposed last season with no pass rush and an over-reliance on Cover-1 and Cover-0.
The secondary has long been an area where general manager Eric DeCosta invests most heavily, and Minter expressed confidence in the overall group Tuesday.
“I feel really good about where were at overall,” he said.

title: Baltimore Ravens Have Two Impact Starters Return To Practice From Injury
full_text:
The rumors of Pro Bowl wide receiver Zay Flowers' demise proved to be greatly exaggerated and the long-awaited return of nose Travis Jones to the field finally arrived Tuesday morning when both were on the practice field at Under Armour Peformance Center when the Baltimore Ravens returned from their day off.
. @ZayFlowers back at practice! pic.twitter.com/MhjuR7h6Xb
Just days after signing the largest deal for a non-quarterback in franchise history , Flowers limped off the practice field with what head coach Jesse Minter revealed was a quad contusion that he sustained after colliding with safety Jaylinn Hawkins during a 7-on-7 drill.
Fans didn't have to wait with bated breath for long, as the only practice Flowers missed was Sunday's under a scorching hot sun. Minter did share that they didn't expect the star wideout to miss much time, stating that he would be "day-to-day" but avid followers of the team had the right to be understandably skeptical given how that term sometimes meant days, weeks and even months under former head coach John Harbaugh.
"I feel really good about where that is at, and I think those types of things may take a couple of days," Minter said Sunday. "It may take one day [or] three days," Minter said. "But, I feel good that he will be back out there being Zay here pretty soon."
Jones, on the other hand, is making his training camp practice debut after passing his physical and being removed from the Physically Unable to Perform list. He missed the first couple of weeks of camp and most of the offseason program while recovering from a reported pectoral injury.
The fifth-year veteran is coming off a career year in which he led the team with a personal-best five sacks and was first among interior defensive linemen in defensive snaps played (743) and total tackles made (47).
He joins two-time Pro Bowler Nnamdi Maduike and veteran nose tackle John Jenkins as the third player from their position group and fifth overall to come off the P.U.P. While six-time Pro Bowl defensive end Calais Campbell didn't open camp on any sort of injury list, he started on a gradual ramp-up and is now taking part in full team 11-on-11 drills.
"Expect that room over the next week to two weeks to really, really take shape for us," Minter said.
Jones' removal from P.U.P leaves second-year inside linebacker Teddye Buchanan as the only one still on the list as he continues his miraculous recovery from a torn ACL.
As great as it is to see the starting and primary backup interior defensive linemen achieve or near full health with just over a month until the start of the regular season, the current depth behind them is shallow and will have its endurance tested this Saturday when the Philadelphia Eagles come to town for an exhibition game at M&T Bank Stadium.
The Ravens also had second-year defensive tackle Aeneas Peebles return to practice on Tuesday after he missed nearly a week with an undisclosed injury. However, they are heading into their first preseason game with the same group of unheralded youngsters who have been grinding away with the first and second team defenses the past fortnight while the more established players have been getting healthy.
Expect to see a lot of Peebles, veteran Broderick Washington, rookies Rayshaun Benny, Aaron Graves and Dion Wilson Jr. as well as second-and-third-year pros David Olajiga and C.J. Okoye, the last two of whom are international pathway players.
Another key injury to monitor heading into the preseason opener is the status of veteran reserve quarterback Skylar Thompson.
He continues to miss practice with an undisclosed injury, and if he can't play against the Eagles, the Ravens will likely only play Pro Bowl backup Tyler Huntley for the first quarter or just a couple of series and will get an extended look at undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano out of UConn.

title: Ravens Rookie EDGE Zion Young Is Progressing Well in Transition to NFL
full_text:
There's a lot that goes into making the leap from competing at the highest level in college football to playing against the best in the world at the professional level. While some first-year pros have a steeper learning curve than others, there are those who take to the increased speed, physicality and need to be more technically proficient faster than most.
Baltimore Ravens second-round rookie outside linebacker Zion Young falls into the latter category as he has been progressing at a steady rate since rookie minicamp, making noticeable strides at every stage along the way.
"He's been improving so much," second-year outside linebacker Mike Green said. "Just a young guy coming straight from college — to come in here and [have] big expectations, he's been taking large leaps. It's just like a typical rookie thing [in that] some guys can get stuck, [but] he's been taking some huge steps, and that's probably the hardest thing you can do as a rookie. He's been great for us so far, and we're excited [about] what he can do for us."
Green knows all about what it's like to be a highly drafted edge defender who was a first-round talent and expected to produce right away because he just did last year after being the Ravens 2025 second-rounder. He was thrust into a larger-than-expected role as a rookie, recording 3.5 sacks, and ended up leading his entire position group in defensive snaps played.
In Young's eyes, the aspect of his game where he has made the most progress since coming in at reporting to rookie camp in early May until now in the first training camp of his pro career is in his alignment at the line of scrimmage.
"In college, it is a lot of offset back' and here is a lot of under center," Young said. "So, [it is] my alignment for the most part, knowing who is beside me and the reason, the whole situation, my whole defense. I am just understanding that."
Even before the Ravens put pads on for the first time last week, the former Missouri Tiger's physicality and power were apparent, and he didn't disappoint once the pads finally did come on. He's been a regular backfield disrupter during practice, living up to his pre-draft prowess as a run defender with several blown-up plays at and behind the line of scrimmage.
ZION YOUNG REP🫣 pic.twitter.com/bJAAmzQTcH
"You just watch him out here, and the way he plays down-in and down-out is unbelievable," Ravens outside linebackers coach Harland Bower said.
Young and the rest of the Ravens rookie will get their first taste of all-out and full-contact NFL action in the team's preseason opener this upcoming Saturday when the Philadelphia Eagles come to town. As amped as he was to put on pads for the first time last week, he's even more fired up to finally put on his full uniform for the first time and get to go up against someone in a different colored jersey.
"I am not where I want to be yet, but knowing the game [is] coming up next week, I am just preparing myself [and] taking it a day at a time," Young said.
While what Young does on the field and puts on film is the final product, he is also conducting himself like a true professional off the field to make sure he can stay on it and be ready to be at his best when his number is called, such as monitoring his diet and getting proper treatment for his body.
"We have good nutritionists here. They set you up," Young said. "They help you be where you want to be. So, it is the same if you are coming from a good college. I came from Missouri, so we had good nutritionists, and we had good athletic training. They held me accountable for the most part. I came here and they are doing the same thing, [holding] me to that standard. So, it has been pretty cool."
Another asset that has been integral in his adjustment to the NFL is his childhood friend and former Westlake High School teammate, cornerback Nate Wiggins. They grew up together in Atlanta, Georgia, remained close and Wiggins has helped him stay on track so that they both can be disruptive forces for the Ravens on defense.
"He has just been holding me accountable," Young said. "The small stuff, just me leaving stuff around my locker, he is holding me accountable. He has always been a fun guy to play with. He is a freakish athlete, so I have had fun playing with him. I am still having fun. It is crazy [that] we are in the NFL together now [on the] same team."

title: Elijah Sarratt May Be The Ravens "Other" Rookie WR For Now, But He's Making Strides Too
full_text:
The Ravens haven’t played a preseason game yet and have had but a handful of padded practices, and already Elijah Sarratt is the “other” rookie wide receiver.
The Baltimore native hasn’t had the string of eye-popping catches as fellow rookie Ja’Kobi Lane and he hasn’t been the subject of growing social media lore and he’s had a perfectly reasonable indoctrination into the very early stages of his NFL career without any setbacks or issues. He just hasn’t been conjuring up perhaps outsized expectations based on practice production, which isn’t a bad thing by any stretch.
The Ravens record of identifying and developing college talent at this position is incredibly sketchy. Their history of having first and second year players create quite a stir in OTAs or the first two weeks of training camp is littered with names who go on to be quickly forgotten. One strongly suspects that neither Lane, their third-round pick, nor Sarratt, a Baltimore native who was their fourth-round pick , fall into either of those buckets. But projecting too much out of what either has done to this point is a tricky proposition as well.
Sarratt, like Lane, isn’t making too much out of how things have gone so far.
Being able to practice everyday and hit the post and learn and absorb is progress. Avoiding the kind of soft tissue problems that can erode a first training camp at this position and earn trust and respect is a quality in and of itself. A lot of the dirty work Sarratt is going to be asked to do won’t come with a highlight reel attached to it, by design, and it’s far too early to be projecting for any of these youngsters.
Both are adopting a commendable outward mindset about the process.
"Just know every day's not going to be perfect,” Sarratt explained. “You're going to have ups and downs, but just continue to find those little ways to get better. You need to be coachable. Number one, you have to be coachable.
“Like I said, there are so many great people in this NFL — defense, offense — and playing against a great defense every single day. So just listening to everybody, trying to earn people's trust and just continue to get better - stack days.”
This weekend will be the first true test for all of the rookies, and these receivers figure to get quite a run.
Hopefully, veteran back-up Skylar Thompson, the third-string QB dealing with what head coach Jesse Minter termed a minor injury, will be able to play against the Eagles. Having him behind presumptive exhibition starter Snoop Huntley will gives these kids a measure of accuracy and veteran presence that will go quite a ways in a setting like this, where quarterback play can be outright rotten and negate the ability to assess the pass catchers.
The Eagles boast one of the premier secondaries in the NFL and not that the top dogs will be playing much, and not that defensive guru Vic Fangio will be throwing a regular-season game plan at them, either, but it’s a quality roster all the way around. This is a real opportunity to begin to separate.
“We have a great group of guys that are invested in being complete receivers,” receivers coach Keary Colbert said of a group that lacks much NFL experience besides Zay Flowers (who won’t play Saturday and is nursing an injury himself) and Rashod Bateman. “And doing whatever it takes to help the offense and help the team. So, I'm excited to watch the guys compete, to block, to catch, to run, to play special teams [and] to do whatever we can to help this organization win.”
Sarratt was a playmaker and chain mover for the national title Indiana Hoosiers and was a go-to guy for quarterback Fernando Mendoza, whom the Raiders drafted first-overall. The St. Francis product knows that doesn’t mean much at all now, and understands it’s going to take a lot to work his way up this depth chart, starting with checking as many boxes as he can Saturday night.
Sarratt needs to find his way in high-traffic situations – which attracted him to front offices and scouts in the pre-draft process – and be able to present an attractive target for Lamar Jackson even if defenders want to drape all over him. The Ravens loved the size that Sarratt (6-2) and Lane (6-4) provide and using them as Jokers to run tight end concepts is certainly something rookie coordinator Declan Doyle – borrowing heavily from his mentor Sean Payton – has in mind
“Windows are a little tighter, so I have to make contested catches,” Sarratt said. “Like, even when someone's on you, you have to have the mentality that you're open still. Yes, windows are a little tighter, like I said, people are a little faster, but football's football. I've been feeling confident going out there. I've been learning from the best, so just keep stacking days."

title: Ravens Banking On Seeing Their First Team DL By Next Week, Just In Time
full_text:
The Baltimore Ravens received the best piece of medical news possible when All Pro defensive tackle Nnamdi Madubuike returned to practice from neck surgery, but through the first few weeks of training camp, that unit has yet to see the field together.
The Ravens are taking every precaution with Madubuike , obviously, and will be very judicious with the types of collisions he is a part of in the preseason. They were lauded for re-signing veteran lineman Calais Campbell, a move we championed well before it took place , but the 40-year old dealt with an unspeakable family tragedy that naturally took precedence over his earliest work back in Owings Mills.
Two veterans who carried a very heavy load last year in Madubuike’s absence – Travis Jones and John Jenkins, opened camp on the Physically Unable to Participate list, compromising their camp. Jenkins has returned but Jones is still overcoming a pec injury – which can be quite tricky especially on an athlete this size – and rookie head coach Jesse Minter, a defensive guru who will be calling plays on that side of the ball – has yet to really see much of his top talents among this all-important position group, let alone see them gelling and interacting as a unit.
That seems likely to be the case by early next week, if not sooner.
The Ravens schedule is already getting bifurcated with the preseason games about to start, and with the team off Monday and then off again Friday before facing the Eagles Saturday, it’s a tricky time to bring players back from long-term injury. Some of the sessions are quite heated to prepare for the games ahead and others are glorified walk throughs. But from the sound of it, Jones will be back in the mix soon and the coaches should start to see how the pieces fit up front.
“I think Travis will (be back) real, real soon, honestly,” Minter said Sunday, “be starting to work back in. It’s been great to get 'Jenk' back in there, Calais [Campbell] back in there. Calais was at Larry Fitzgerald's Hall of Fame ceremony (over the weekend), so we excused him from practice, but was great to see him back in the team periods - a few reps today, and John as well. Expect that room over the next week to two weeks to really, really take shape for us."
Indeed, hopefully that will be the case, because time is starting to run a little thin. Days off around the preseason games start to replicate more of a regular season schedule, time will be lost to travel, too, and even with so many of these absent players having a strong understanding of this defense and the core principles – Minter is running something very close to what Mike Macdonald ran here in 2022-2023 – there is no substitute for feeling things out together and starting to bond as a group.
And on the edge, this is new terrain for top pass rusher Trey Hendrickson and second-round pick Zion Young, and the more they can replicate twists and stunts and moves together up front the better. Getting a look at certain NASCAR packages and toggling different body types rushing from the inside has been virtually impossible to this point given the variance in the personnel availability and this is a group that absolutely must perform at a level far above what took place last season .
Minter lit up when talking about what it’s been like getting Campbell, still quite versatile in how he can be deployed, and Jenkins – a big space eater – back on the field. Their absence has allowed the team to get a nice look at players like seventh-round pick Rayshaun Benny, who we believe will surprise this season . But the closer we get to Week 1 the more uneasy any coach would get, let alone a first-time head coach who also runs the defense, not getting to see his first-team defensive line aligned.
“Both of them — just experience, physicality, size, length, the ability to impact the game both in the run and the pass,” Minter said of that veteran duo. “Great to have them back out there. It has been awesome, I would say, for some of the guys to get the amount of reps that they have gotten.
“I think they have all gotten better and taken advantage of that. So, as we get these guys back, I think that room will just become even better and more deep as a result of some of those guys missing a little bit of time."

title: Devontez Walker Isn’t Threatened by Presence of Ravens Promising Rookie WRs
full_text:
During his first two years in the league, targets and even offensive snaps were hard to come by for Baltimore Ravens wide receiver Devontez Walker . In each of those offseasons, the team either re-signed or brought in a new established veteran to round out the top three spots on their depth chart at the position.
When he was a rookie in 2024, the Ravens brought back Nelson Agholor for a second season, and last season, they signed five-time Pro Bowler DeAndre Hopkins, both of whom finished either second or third at the position in receptions, receiving yards, touchdowns and offensive snaps played.
There was never really a competition to be had for the No. 3 receiver role during that time, as both veterans were penciled into that role from pretty much the start given their experience and well-rounded skillsets.
Meanwhile, Walker made the most of the limited opportunities to contribute on offense during that span by recording four touchdowns and three first downs on six of his seven career receptions. He emerged as a potent yet underutilized deep threat last year by averaging 22.7 yards per catch and finished with a career-high 136 receiving yards after recording just one catch for a 21-yard scoring strike as a rookie.
The Ravens didn't retain or look to add another notable veteran wideout to impede Walker's ascension up the depth chart and prevent him from carving out a larger role for himself in the offense. However, they did bring in a pair of talented rookies in the middle rounds of the 2026 NFL Draft to compete with him and replenish their ranks at the position after not bringing back Hopkins and letting veteran special teams ace Tylan Wallace sign elsewhere in free agency.
In the third round, they selected former USC standout Ja'Kobi Lane , who has been the unrivaled star of training camp thus far and is looking like the biggest threat to him assuming the No. 3 receiver mantle. With their first pick on Day 3, they took former Indiana standout Elijah Sarratt , who is fresh off winnng a national title and has been coming on strong in camp as of late, the healthier he's gotten.
Even with Lane's hot start to camp and Sarratt starting to heat up, Walker isn't fazed by the presence of either first-year pro and is instead more focused on continuing his own strong start to his third training camp as he's been consistently making plays in practice as well.
"[I'm] just coming out here and making sure I do the things I need to do to be a part of the offense," Walker said Sunday. "I understand, [the team] brought those guys in, and they are going to be a part of what we have going on — just making sure I continue to do the things to be a part of what we are trying to accomplish."
Count Walker among the many outspoken players who have expressed their excitement about the new scheme and direction that first-year offensive coordinator Declan Doyle is implementing, and he feels like he's acclimating to it pretty well so far.
"I feel really good about it," Walker said. "Being here throughout the spring, [I] did not really miss a day, trying to get comfortable with it — I feel pretty comfortable with it right now. Our coaches are doing a good job with making us as comfortable as possible with it.
"I like [Doyle] a lot. [He is a] good dude, [and] he is big on bringing the offense together, being pretty tight-knit. Then, [I] also [like] the intent he has on perfecting the offense so we can hit the ground running when we get to the game."
While Wallace was able to find a new home in free agency by joining former Ravens offensive coordinator Todd Monken with the Cleveland Browns, Hopkins has yet to do the same, and instead of waiting around for a team to call, he has chosen to stay busy by getting a jumpstart on his coaching career.
In late July, he announced that he isn't retiring from the NFL but that he will be occupying his time until he can resume playing by grooming and giving back to the next generation as an assistant wide receiver coach at the collegiate level under Brent Key at Georgia Tech University.
I Haven’t retired from the @NFL … But if you're a WR and you want to be great, come to @GeorgiaTechFB
This news came as a surprise to Walker, who believes that Hopkins can still contribute and play at a high level. Even though the 13-year veteran posted the lowest totals of his career across the board, he got off to a hot start before injuries began derailing every aspect of the offense outside of Zay Flowers and Derrick Henry, and he still managed to come up with timely clutch catches no matter who was under center at quarterback.
"I think he can still play," Walker said. "'D-Hop' was one of those guys who was really good for me, and I feel like every time he was out there, he made a lot of plays," Walker said.
As a former University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill Tar Heel, Walker isn't the biggest fan of where Hopkins chose to begin this next chapter with the Yellow Jackets, a former ACC rival; he's happy for him nonetheless.
"[I] do not love where he ended up — at Georgia Tech — but, I am happy he got that opportunity," Walker said. "Hopefully, he does get back on the field."

title: Nine Surprises Spotted on Buffalo Bills' First Preseason Depth Chart
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills released their unofficial depth chart heading into their August 15 preseason opener against the Carolina Panthers in Orchard Park, and there are more than a few surprises.
Of course, to no one's surprise five-time NFL MVP finalist Josh Allen sits in the QB1 slot, but there's real interest in the battle to be his understudy.
The backup quarterback competition is one of multiple spots that will be determined over the next few weeks.
With two weeks of training camp practices in the books, here are the nine positions that caught our attention when examining the first depth chart.
Bills' First Released Depth Chart (Preseason Week 1) 👀 [ @BuffaloBillsPR ] pic.twitter.com/Z1B0Jlbh0e
Mitch Trubisky is gone, and two familiar faces are vying to replace him. Kyle Allen, who was QB2 for the Bills in 2023, returns to compete against Shane Buechele, who has spent three seasons with Buffalo, primarily in a practice squad role.
Allen holds second-team status on the depth chart, but neither has been overly impressive during open camp practices. The preseason games will go a long way in determining the winner.
Despite Josh Palmer's strong start to training camp, the Bills have listed embattled 2024 second-round pick Keon Coleman as the third wide receiver when starting the game in trips formation.
Palmer is listed on the second team, directly behind WR1 DJ Moore. Fourth-round rookie Skyler Bell currently stands as Coleman's backup.
The Bills deployed fullback Reggie Gilliam for 21 percent of offensive snaps in 2025. Despite Gilliam's departure, it's presumed Buffalo desires to keep a fullback in its bag of tricks.
The decision will be between undrafted rookie Jackson Acker and former Philadelphia Eagles' converted linebacker Ben Van Sumeren, who is currently first on the depth chart. The real test will be how each competitor responds in the run game during live preseason action. It's worth noting that Acker was contributor for Wisconsin under interim head coach Jim Leonhard , who is now the Bills' defensive coordinator.
With Davis Edwards landing a mega contract with the New Orleans Saints, the Bills need to settle on a new starting left guard. Utilityman Alec Anderson, who has spent the past two seasons as Buffalo's sixth lineman, entered as a slight favorite and holds first-team status ahead of the preseason opener.
Veteran free agent addition Austin Corbett, the starting right guard for the Super Bowl LVI champion Los Angeles Rams, is the primary challenger to Anderson . He's second on the depth chart with undrafted rookie Bruno Fina on the third team.
The three first-team down linemen include two second-year players. While Deone Walker is the presumed nose tackle, fellow 2025 pick TJ Sanders is listed at defensive end opposite veteran Ed Oliver .
The second-team trio consists of a bulked-up Landon Jackson and fifth-round round Zane Durant on the ends with former Washington Commanders' second-rounder Phidarian Mathis in the middle. In a troubling sign for Dewayne Carter , who is coming off an Achilles tear, the 2024 third-round pick is on the third team behind nose tackles Walker and Mathis.
It doesn't appear as if the unsigned Matt Milano will return, meaning the Bills need a starter to pair with two-time returning captain Terrel Bernard. Despite what's been an impressive showing thus far from fourth-round rookie Kaleb Elarms-Orr, returnee Dorian Williams is listed next to Bernard on the first team.
Elarms-Orr is the current second-teamer behind Williams while Joe Andreessen is backing up Bernard. Keonta Jenkins and Jimmy Ciarlo are the third-teamers.
With Cole Bishop, who is coming off a breakout season, entering camp as an incumbent starter, there is a loaded competition for the spot alongside him. Three veterans, all with prior NFL starting experience, are in the mix along with a rookie.
Chauncey Gardner-Johnson, a Super Bowl LIX champion, is the current leader . Meanwhile, familiar veteran Damar Hamlin and free-agent addition Geno Stone are listed on the second team. Hamlin is behind Gardner-Johnson with Stone backing up Bishop. Notably, Fifth-round rookie Jalon Kilgore, who generated some buzz before the pads came on, currently holds third-team status.
The burning question here is who will earn the spot playing opposite CB1 Christian Benford? Right now, the odds are trending in Max Hairston's favor with the 2025 first-round draft pick listed on the first team. After beginning his rookie season on Injured Reserve, Hairston eventually earned three starts before a different injury sidelined him for the playoffs.
Second-round rookie Davison Igbinosun, who is viewed as Hairston's main competitor , holds second-team status behind Benford. Meanwhile, undrafted rookie Kani Walker, who has been one of the top surprises of camp thus far, is listed behind Hairston.
While returnee Mitch Wishnowsky was seemingly put on notice when the Bills used a seventh-round draft pick on rookie Tommy Doman, the 34-year-old veteran currently holds an incumbency advantage.
Wishnowsky enters the preseason lid-lifter as the Bills' primary punter and holder.

title: Bills’ Rookie Skyler Bell Being Held Back in Buffalo’s WR Battle
full_text:
Despite being the second player selected by the Buffalo Bills in the fourth round of the 2026 NFL Draft in April—and the fourth player in the overall pecking order of the team’s 10-player draft class this spring—there may have been no player that received greater hype entering their first NFL offseason over the past few months leading up to training camp in Pittsford, New York, than rookie wide receiver Skyler Bell, who was quickly snatched up by the Bills at pick No. 125 out of the University of Connecticut on Day 3 of the league-wide event four months ago.
Bell was instantly beloved by many in Bills Mafia . . . and he felt it.
“It’s just motivation. I want to show people (around the league that)—y’all [expletive] up—I’m really that (guy),” Bills’ rookie receiver Skyler Bell said in an interview with The Buffalo News earlier this offseason.
“I’m just trying to get better every day. So, when the season comes, I’m ready to put it all together."
The wide receiver position has seemingly always been a hot-button topic of discussion in Western New York in recent years, especially since the departure of former veteran All-Pro wide receiver Stefon Diggs in 2024.
And, the outside noise has only grown louder with the recent struggles of third-year wideout Keon Coleman and last year’s top free-agent signing Joshua Palmer, who’s a former 2021 third-round draft pick of the Los Angeles Chargers out of the University of Tennessee.
Combine that with the fact that Bell finished second in the entire FBS in 2025 with 1,278 receiving yards and 13 receiving touchdowns on 101 receptions for the Huskies, and it’s not hard to see why the anticipation to finally witness him on the field this offseason had been mounting from fans.
The Bronx, New York, native, who originally attended the University of Wisconsin from 2021 to 2023 before transferring to Connecticut in 2024, was simply sensational as a senior while playing for UConn this past fall. And, with that in mind, many outside observers thought that the transition of going from catching passes from former Huskies quarterback Joe Fagnano in college to being the recipient of balls supplied by Bills’ franchise quarterback Josh Allen in the pros would be seamless.
So far, however, that has not been the case for the 5-foot-11, 192-pound wideout this summer through the first slate of practices at training camp .
It hasn’t been due to too much fault of his own, though.
Bell, who—at the age of 24—is actually older than Coleman despite being a rookie, and is just two years younger than the previously aforementioned 26-year-old Palmer, hasn’t been receiving much time catching passes from Allen thus far in August at all.
Instead, it’s been backup quarterbacks Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele throwing the rookie receiver the “rock” as both players are currently in a battle for the right to be Buffalo’s former 2024 league MVP’s backup this season.
And, with that being the case, it has seemingly hindered Bell’s development as he no longer looks like the odds-on favorite to win a top rotational spot on the wide receiver depth chart this fall in his first professional season.
While he got off to a nice start at St. John Fisher University two weeks ago, things have since cooled off quite significantly for the once highly-favored rookie.
In fact, he’s missed the last couple of practices to start this week due to an undisclosed injury, as well, which included Tuesday’s morning session in Orchard Park, New York.
Clearly, it hasn’t been ideal.
But, his offensive coaches aren’t giving up on him: not in the slightest. They’ve seen incremental improvements when Bell’s been between the white lines.
“Yeah, I think that we have thrown a ton at him. We’ve put him at a ton of different positions, (and had him run) a ton of different routes. I mean—we have asked him to do a lot—and he has gone out there, and he’s done everything we’ve asked. He’s smart. He can play those multiple positions. He can run a lot of routes,” new Bills’ offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael Jr. said in an interview at One Bills Drive on Monday.
“I think that, again, maybe the last couple days there just hasn’t been (a connection). He’s been open, and maybe there are (misreads) . . . (or) I should say that maybe (the coach) called the play to get him the ball, and a specific coverage took it to somebody else. . . .
“We’re excited with where he’s at.”
On that note, the fact that Bell is being relegated to practicing mostly with the second- and third- string offenses so far in camp appears to be due to a combination of things.
First, the adjustment period from making the jump from playing at a somewhat smaller—at least in terms of football—school at the collegiate level to playing in the NFL might be taking a little longer than initially expected.
And, that’s OK: it’s normal.
However, what’s more concerning is his inability to earn more increased reps with the starting unit through his play in practice.
Is it due to Kyle Allen and Shane Buechele’s incompetency, which Carmichael somewhat tried to avoid mentioning in his interview, or is it due to a lack of current comfortability?
Whatever the case may be, Bell hasn’t blown anyone away in Buffalo so far.
He’ll need a string of strong preseason performances to end the summer if he’s going to earn the right to see the field for any significant amount of time in his rookie campaign, at least early on.
Right now, Coleman and Palmer appear to be firmly entrenched on the depth chart ahead of the “youngster” heading into Saturday’s exhibition opener against the Carolina Panthers on Saturday at 1:00 p.m. ET at the new $2.1 billion Highmark Stadium , and it’ll be up to Bell to change that.
If not, his rookie year might go off the rails before it even gets started. But, it’s not time to panic just yet, either.
First, he must get back on the field quickly. And, if can get back in time—once Saturday rolls around—the former Taft School standout must show up and show out in his NFL preseason debut.
And, Carmichael Jr. —despite there being many outside opinions to the contrary—believes that his backup quarterbacks can give Bell the chance that he needs to shine.
“I think that they both bring a ton of value—not only on the field—but what they bring to the meeting room, their relationship with Josh, their ability to communicate with him, and kind of from their vision, too: what they see,” Carmichael Jr. added on Monday.
“But, I think that—as we get into the preseason and play some games—it’ll be a great opportunity to see them both.”
Hopefully, it’ll be a great opportunity for the once highly-anticipated rookie receiver, as well.
Fans will soon find out. The preseason opener is just days away from taking place in Western New York.
It’s almost time to celebrate some more, Bills Mafia .

title: Buffalo Bills Respond After Widespread Complaints About New Highmark Stadium
full_text:
What was supposed to be a celebration quickly turned into a list of concerns. The Buffalo Bills hosted fans for the first time at their new Highmark Stadium this past Saturday as they held their annual Return of the Blue & Red practice .
There was an attendance record set as more than 50,000 fans packed the new stadium and watched the Bills' scrimmage. While there were plenty of positive aspects to take in , social media was buzzing with complaints.
Some of the biggest concerns involved seats that had obstructed views , which does happen at times at stadiums, but many fans felt they were misinformed before purchasing their season tickets. Another major complaint was the size of the video boards , which were on the smaller side for a stadium that exceeded $2 billion.
The Bills have heard the complaints and decided there were sufficient concerns that they should respond. For that reason, they released a statement, saying that they will utilize the next six weeks to address and refine any details possible.
"Thank you to Bills Mafia for setting a new attendance record with more than 50,000 fans at the Return of the Blue & Red. Saturday's practice was a great opportunity to test the new stadium. We are currently addressing internal and external feedback regarding the facility's operation following the first event. We'll utilize the next six weeks to refine any details as we prepare for the home opener on Thursday, September 17,” the Bills said in a statement via ESPN’s Alaina Getzenberg .
Initially, that statement makes it sound as though the front office is going to see what changes can be made. That said, later comments relayed by Getzenberg suggest otherwise.
In her piece, Getzenberg quotes a source saying that the team heard from "less than 1% of PSL holders" about issues with the view. They also said some of the pictures being shared were from seats that are not designed for football events.
This isn't to say that no changes will be made, but it sounds as though the powers that be might not believe the concerns are valid enough to make sweeping alterations. That said, it's also highly illogical to believe that any significant changes can be made to such a massive product in a mere six weeks. Instead, some fans will have to deal with some inconveniences and small video boards.

title: Former Bills’ Safeties Micah Hyde, George Wilson Return to Football With New Gigs
full_text:
Without a shadow of a doubt, it’s been a whirlwind in Western New York since that fateful day in January this past winter following the Buffalo Bills’ divisional-round debacle that took place against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colorado, back on January 17.
Tears were shed in the locker room. Concerns were voiced at the podium through the media.
And, in the end, changes—which some might deem seismic—were made by Bills’ owner Terry Pegula this offseason.
But, sometimes change is good— sometimes it’s needed —because introducing a fresh perspective never hurts .
However, even with that said, there are at least a few faces making their way back into the lives of Bills Mafia everywhere this upcoming fall that fans will recognize quite well.
There will be at least some familiarity coming to people’s screens again starting this August.
How do those few sayings go again?
“Absence makes the heart grow fonder .” “ All roads lead home.” Yada yada: well, whatever phrase fans might fancy that carries a similar meaning, it would certainly hold true this summer for the Western New York organization and a few of its former players.
Back in July, Bills ON SI covered the story of how former Bills’ center Mitch Morse is making a move from being a one-time NFL offensive lineman to now covering the team this fall on the franchise’s radio program with analyst Chris Trapasso.
And, when the announcement was made, it was certainly a full-circle moment for Morse.
But now, in addition to the 6-foot-6, 305-pound longtime pivot man making his way into the media sphere, it was recently announced that two other former Bills’ greats are also set to join him on the screen and in the airwaves of the Buffalo media landscape this upcoming preseason, regular season, and—hopefully—the postseason.
One is a recent fan favorite, while the other is a face that many Bills Mafia members will remember from when that term wasn’t even relevant.
Former Bills’ safeties Micah Hyde and George Wilson.
Hyde, who signed on with the team via free agency in 2017 with—at that point in time—Buffalo’s rookie head coach Sean McDermott before going on to play seven total seasons in Orchard Park (2017-2023) , will be joining the Buffalo Plus podcast on YouTube with reporters Jenna Cottrell, Dan Fetes, and Mike Catalana of the 13WHAM TV station in Rochester, New York.
It will be a weekly appearance during the season for Hyde, which comes on the heels of his brief return to Buffalo’s practice squad in December 2024.
The one-time Iowa Hawkeye, who also played for the Green Bay Packers (2013-2016) before joining the Bills, is a native of Fostoria, Ohio, and finished his NFL career with 644 total tackles, 66 pass deflections, 24 interceptions, 18 tackles for loss, nine fumble recoveries, eight quarterback hits, five sacks, four forced fumbles, and one interception returned for a touchdown in 158 career regular season games according to Pro Football Reference .
In 17 postseason appearances, the 6-foot, 197-pound playmaking defensive back had 69 combined tackles, nine pass breakups, two interceptions, two quarterback hits, one sack, one forced fumble, and one fumble recovery to his name.
It was an illustrious professional playing career for Hyde, to say the least, and now he’s ready to tackle his next post-NFL opportunity, which consists of being an attentive husband and father of three, as well as now covering a team on a weekly basis that he says was the one football organization that he’ll always consider himself a part of—for life—even if his current personal and professional habits are changing on the daily.
“I’ve been busier now than I’ve ever been in my life. (My wife and I) had our third child three months ago, so she’s keeping us on our toes,” former Bills’ safety turned media analyst Micah Hyde said during his first appearance on the Buffalo Plus podcast on August 5.
“I’m coaching flag football this year guys, (too). . . . We’ll see how it goes . . . but you guys are going to hear about it all year. I’m excited for you guys because there’s going to be some funny stories, and you guys will get to be very, very entertained. . . . I wish I had more years to help out the Bills organization, but unfortunately (I) was not able to . . . but I’ll always remember myself as ‘23’ for the Buffalo Bills.
“And, my whole family—even a lot of my friends and former teammates I was in Buffalo with—still call me ‘23’, right? So, that’s part of my identity (now).”
On that note, in addition to Hyde, the other former Bills’ safety joining the media ranks in Western New York this offseason—George Wilson—is also excited to get started with his latest professional endeavor, which will be as a co-host with Buffalo’s current team reporter Maddy Glab for a new Bills’ pregame and halftime show from inside the stadium on game days.
Wilson, a former undrafted free-agent signing of the Detroit Lions from the University of Arkansas who transitioned to safety once in the NFL en route to playing nine seasons with Buffalo from 2004 to 2012, will also be a part of the team’s postgame programming, which will be broadcast on Buffalo’s various social media platforms.
Much like it was previously mentioned with Morse and Hyde, it’s a surreal moment for the 45-year-old Paducah, Kentucky, native, who finished his NFL playing career with 526 total tackles, 14 interceptions, six quarterback hits, five fumble recoveries, four-and-a-half sacks, three forced fumbles, and one interception returned for a touchdown in 124 career games.
Wilson, whose former teammates nicknamed “The Senator” , also played two seasons with the Tennessee Titans in 2013 and 2014.
He was also teammates with current Bills’ defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard while the two played in Buffalo together from 2005 to 2007, so there’s certainly no shortage of precious intimate information to go around from the former 6-foot, 210-pound collegiate receiver turned NFL defender.
Unlike Hyde and Morse, however, Wilson never experienced the high that comes along with playoff football during his playing days.
So, needless to say, this upcoming season is—if all things play out right—going to be an absolute treat to watch, and talk about, for the one-time Arkansas Razorback, Buffalo Bill, and Tennessee Titan playmaker.
“You guys (in Western New York) have always welcomed me with open arms, and I’m just excited to be back in the fold in an official capacity and just be a part of the team as we go into the new stadium.
“This outlook on the season’s great, and (I’m) just excited to be back around the organization and in the Western New York community,” George Wilson said when speaking on One Bills Live with hosts Chris Brown and Steve Tasker on Thursday, August 6, following the conclusion of Buffalo’s second to last training camp session at St. John Fisher University in Pittsford, New York, at the end of last week.
“I’ve seen it on television, but now—to be able to do it and experience it myself—it’s something I’m looking forward to: adding to the game-day experience for Bills Mafia as they come and see our beloved Bills play on Sundays. . . . I’m just excited to be back.”
Wilson’s first opportunity will come in short order.
Despite the fanbase’s incredible record turnout for the “Return of the Blue & Red” scrimmage in Buffalo’s southeastern suburb on August 8, the Bills will officially kick the preseason off this upcoming Saturday at the team’s brand new $2.1 billion Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, New York, with a game against the Carolina Panthers.
Kickoff for the exhibition matchup is slated for 1:00 p.m. ET.

title: Five Buffalo Bills Who Need a Strong Preseason Debut vs. Panthers
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills had their first showing at the new Highmark Stadium on Saturday as they hosted fans for their annual Return of the Blue & Red Scrimmage. This weekend, they will play against an opposing team for the first time in their new home.
This Saturday, Buffalo welcomes the Carolina Panthers in Week 1 of the preseason . Neither team is likely to play many starters, but the preseason is never focused on the star players.
Instead, the exhibition games give players on the roster bubble a chance to prove they deserve to make the team. That being the case, here are five Bills who need to stand out against Carolina to improve their chances of making the 53-man roster.
Veteran Mike Danna spent the past six seasons with the Kansas City Chiefs and had a standout campaign in 2023 with 6.5 sacks. Entering 2026, he's on the bubble with the Bills and has to prove he's a superior option to Javon Solomon. This Saturday will be a great chance for him to gain an advantage.
With Connor McGovern out, the Bills will turn to Lloyd Cushenberry as the starter at center, but Sedrick Van Pran-Granger will have a chance to prove he deserves to be in the conversation. Cushenberry has the experience advantage, but Pran-Granger has the chemistry with the team. He can use that on Saturday to make a case for himself.
Mecole Hardman Jr. seemed to be destined for a spot as a wide receiver and kick returner, but he suddenly has competition from Dante Pettis. Signed after a tryout early in camp , Pettis has made several impressive plays during practices and could give the Bills a spark in the passing game.
He's also shown promise as a return man, averaging 8.5 yards on punt returns and 24.8 yards on kick returns the past two seasons with the New Orleans Saints. Hardman has the advantage since he was with the franchise in 2025, but Pettis can close the gap with a strong preseason debut.
Kyle Allen was signed this offseason as a replacement for Mitchell Trubisky, who left in free agency. Allen, who started his career with the Carolina Panthers in 2018, played for Buffalo in 2023 and was the primary reserve behind Josh Allen. He was expected to reclaim that spot, but a shaky camp has his spot in jeopardy. This weekend, he has a chance to ease concerns if he can put together a solid outing against his former team.
With Kyle Allen struggling, Shane Buechele had a golden opportunity to supplant him as the No. 2 guy. Unfortunately, he's also had his struggles during camp and hasn't been able to capitalize. He could tilt things in his favor, however, should he outperform Allen on Saturday.

title: Bills Need Overlooked Signing to Bail Out Offensive Line After Connor McGovern Injury
full_text:
It certainly helps when the next man up has 80 career NFL starts under his belt.
The Buffalo Bills ' offensive line absorbed a blow during Saturday's Return of the Blue & Red practice , which was open to ticketed spectators at the brand-new Highmark Stadium.
Starting center Connor McGovern, who signed a four-year contract extension this past offseason, left the nighttime practice, and he did not return. The 28-year-old McGovern was one of three Bills' players , by our count, to go off due to injury on August 8.
Replacing McGovern, veteran center Lloyd Cushenberry stepped up to take the first-team reps. The Bills signed Cushenberry, who had made 80 regular season starts since 2020, in March after the Tennessee Titans released the six-year starter with a failed physical designation.
"The center position, outside of the quarterback, is the hardest position on the offensive side of the ball. You gotta do everything," said first-year head coach Joe Brady at his post-practice press conference.
It happened during 11-on-11 team drills.
Chasing the play on an interception return, McGovern appeared to pull up lame near the sideline at the 30. He eventually threw his helmet off and went to the ground where he was examined by medical personnel.
Not long thereafter, McGovern was spotted walking gingerly toward the locker room while favoring his right leg.
Although Brady offered no update on Saturday night, the speculation is that McGovern has a mild hamstring strain. The average timetable for return is 2-4 weeks.
Despite McGovern needing to become acclimated with a new starting left guard, which remains to be determined, the Bills would be smart to sideline the Pro Bowl center until Week 1 preparations begin.
After an off-day, the Bills returned to practice indoors on Monday, and McGovern was not seen participating during the session , which was open to media.
The good news is that Buffalo has multiple viable options behind McGovern at center.
"I feel really good [about our center depth]. We've had personnel meetings as a staff and talked about just different roles for different guys. We feel pretty good about with where we're at," said offensive coordinator Pete Carmichael prior to Monday's practice.
When the Bills signed Cushenberry following the initial wave of free agency, we wrote about the perceived importance of general manager Brandon Beane's under-the-radar move , which was met by resounding approval from Brady.
"Lloyd's a starting center in the NFL. You go through the process, going into free agency, there was a chance we lost both Connor and David [Edwards]. It was keeping me up at night with some of those thoughts. Lloyd was a guy, I know he's coming off of an injury, but Lloyd was a possibility of being our starter, or just a guy that we would think about as a starter," said Brady at the NFL spring meetings.
The 28-year-old Cushenberry, a 2020 third-round pick by the Denver Broncos, suffered a torn Achilles midway through the 2024 season with Tennessee. He managed to bounce back to the tune of 15 starts last year, but a labrum tear reportedly caused the Titans to cut ties.
Meanwhile, Sedrick Van Pran-Granger, a 2024 fifth-round draft pick , will also factor into the mix at center. Prior to spending two years in a reserve role with the Bills, he was a three-year starter for the Georgia Bulldogs.
"The fact that we have a guy like Lloyd that has a lot of stripes and has played a lot of football, and we got a guy like Sed that has been just progressing as he's been here. We have a lot of confidence in that," said Brady. "Credit Beane, in these situations that we have guys that aren't just rookies having to go in there and kind of go with it."
While both Alec Anderson and Austin Corbett have experience at the position, it doesn't appear as if the Bills are currently interested in pulling either of them away from the starting left guard competition .

title: Bills' Injury List Grows at Monday's Training Camp Practice
full_text:
Early in camp, the Buffalo Bills were able to survive a major injury scare. Safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson had to be carted off the practice field with a leg injury, but it was later revealed to be a calf strain and nothing major.
Gardner-Johnson has since returned and Go Long’s Tyler Dunne suggested a new approach from rookie head coach Joe Brady should be applauded. The positive news surrounding Gardner-Johnson reminded Dunne that Brady was leaning into the sports science department in an effort to minimize injuries.
"The Bills haven’t suffered the injuries of other teams across the league. As promised, Brady is leaning into his sports science department. While the data’s always been in the system on how best to incorporate various practice strategies to mitigate injuries, that data wasn’t always put to use years past," Dunne wrote.
Unfortunately, for Buffalo, there have been several more injuries since then. The Bills had three players suffer some form of injury during their Return of the Blue & Red scrimmage, including Ty Johnson, Connor McGovern, and Cole Bishop.
After taking Sunday off, the Bills were back at practice on Monday. One thing that stood out during the latest session is how many players were not participating.
According to Matt Parrino of Syracuse.com, eight players were missing including the three who were injured on Saturday.
As Parrino noted, Johnson was out there with a sleeve on his leg but eventually left practice altogether.
Buffalo’s front office has been quiet, giving very little information on each player. That said, the McGovern injury has the chance to be the most impactful given his importance to this offensive line.
Rookie Skyler Bell has the most to lose, however, as he’s in the middle of a battle for his spot in a crowded wide receiver room. As for Cole Bishop and Maxwell Hairston, their injury history is a cause for concern with both players struggling with durability early in their respective careers.
Buffalo let out a sigh of relief when C.J. Gardner-Johnson’s calf strain proved to be minor. Monday, they began holding their breath once again.
Gardner-Johnson made a diving play to break up a pass and stayed down for a spell. He eventually left the field on his own power, but was limping and was checked out by trainers .
The veteran safety has been one of the best defenders at Bills camp, and with Bishop already banged up, the Bills have to be concerned.

title: More Evidence Shows Bills Beat Guard Market With O'Cyrus Torrence Contract
full_text:
O'Cyrus Torrence is, of course, coming off a huge weekend , signing a massive extension with the Buffalo Bills . But he was not the only guard who struck it rich.
Titans standout Peter Skoronski scored a record-setting deal Friday , worth $100 million and a league-high $25 million Average Annual Value (AAV) for his position. For Torrence and Skoronski's sakes, it pays well to be a massive human being who can keep QBs clean.
One thing's for certain with these deals: offensive linemen are a commodity. Both are in the top 10 highest-paid guards in terms of total contract value and AAV, with no player in that group making less than $75 million in contract value or an AAV of $19 million.
Headlines: — A look at Fitz’s legendary career https://t.co/H1hcEQl71N — Skoronski gets paid https://t.co/D6ZraIsTa6 — Torrence gets paid, too https://t.co/eaU0RhzrS3 — No Mahomes for the preseason opener https://t.co/QDSUA6iCae
Torrence was not in line to reset the guard market the way Skoronski did, but he sure did earn himself a favorable deal. Ranking eighth in the league in guard AAV ($19.6 million) and ninth in total contract value ($78.4 million), he is set up to be one of the top-paid guards in the NFL for the foreseeable future.
The two players are now locked up through at least 2030. Considering their play and their ages, both deals make sense from team investment standpoints.
Torrence is 26 and will be turning 27 during the NFL postseason. He's started 50 of his 51 games with the Bills, helping clear the way for the rushing champion in James Cook in 2025 and the league MVP in Josh Allen in 2024.
Skoronski, who turned 25 this summer, has not had as much team success in his career. But he is coming off a 2025 season in which he was rated PFF's sixth-highest guard with a grade of 79.0.
Through the 2025 season, Torrence's 2023 All-Rookie Team selection is the only accolade between the two. But Skoronski's strong 2025 campaign, according to PFF, is greater than any season Torrence has recorded thus far.
Torrence has stayed in the same range of grades in his three seasons. But his best season was in 2025 , posting an overall grade of 59.8. He's shown to be a capable pass protector, earning a pass-blocking grade of 64.0, 32nd in the league.
But the second-highest on that list in 2025 was Skoronski, with a grade of 84.5. He also notched a run-blocking grade of 73.2.
Above all, though, both players are massive presences in the trenches for their respective franchises. Even if Skoronski looks like the better player on paper, that does not diminish Torrence's value as an integral starter for a championship contender like Buffalo.

title: Determining Most Appealing Buffalo Bills' Road Trip on 2026 NFL Schedule
full_text:
The Buffalo Bills ' home games will be extra special in 2026, with it being the first year at the new Highmark Stadium , but that won't take away what will be a very fun year for road games.
Time is winding down on the Bills' first game of the season, which is at Houston. Other destinations are appealing for their own reasons, whether for the cities' spectacle, history or something else. But which game looks like the best to go to?
Before the criteria are explained, I'll say that I've excluded each of the Bills' games against the AFC East because people can travel to these games every year and know what to expect.
I've come up with four categories for each of the sites to measure which one is the best. The highest score wins. Now, let's get started with the first category:
For approximately every 250 miles a city is from Buffalo, I deducted one point from a 1-10 scale, which is the scale I'll generally use.
A game being close to home can be a deal-breaker for fans because of convenience and pricing. However, unlike in 2025, when Buffalo traveled to Pittsburgh and Cleveland, the Bills' 2026 slate doesn't have a location within 11 hours of driving, meaning flying will almost be necessary to get to these games.
Driving to Green Bay and Minneapolis may be feasible, but considering distance and possible rough weather, it'll be harder to drive to the other cities .
This category was calculated based on when the Bills play opponents and their connections to potential playoff seeding. For example, a game against a non-conference opponent early in the season will rank lower than a game against a conference foe late in the year when the playoff race heats up.
Houston may be in Week 1, but it is a game that could mean a lot down the stretch in terms of playoff seeding. The Rams may be a top team, but they are in the opposite conference, so it's not as important as one may think.
Las Vegas and Minnesota are still relatively early in the schedule, but Green Bay in December can be a tough game. Still, Denver is as big a challenge as one can get, as it's a rematch of the divisional-round game that sent the Bills packing.
This category was calculated based on the opponent in general and how they will perform in a season. The better the opponent, the higher the ranking given the Bills' hope for a Super Bowl.
The Texans haved bested the Bills in six consecutive matchups in Houston, while the Rams are the favorites to win it all. The Raiders are rebuilding, while the Vikings seem destined for mediocrity with their revolving door at quarterback and strong defense.
The Packers look to have all their key pieces, including edge rusher Micah Parsons, back by December, and return as one of the NFL's best then. Finally, Denver will be looking to prove that last season's run to the AFC Championship Game was not a fluke.
Seeing how advanced stadiums have come is always a thing of beauty, even if it costs a pretty penny to get inside one. Many of the stadiums Buffalo will travel to are some of the best in the league , with three of them (Allegiant Stadium in Vegas, U.S. Bank Stadium in Minneapolis and SoFi Stadium in Inglewood) introduced in 2016 or later.
As for the others, Empower Field at Mile High has a stadium built for excellent Denver sunsets like the one that will come on Christmas Day when the Bills are in town, and NRG Stadium in Houston has a retractable roof that makes it suitable for any game day . Finally, Lambeau Field's pageantry and old-school background make it the gold standard for what the NFL is about.
This category was calculated based on what else there is to do in the city, although I did it on a 1-5 scale with the thinking that people who go will focus on the game and not what else to do before if they go for a long weekend.
Houston has the Space Center and Los Angeles is the entertainment capital of the world, though going to L.A. may leave you wanting more, as I did a bit when I traveled there for a couple days in April.
Las Vegas has its famous strip and the Sphere, and considering the Bills are traveling to Denver around Christmas, skiing and the Rocky Mountain National Park are a couple of attractions that would make an extended holiday visit a great time.
Meanwhile, Minneapolis is not known for much besides great nature and it being the biggest city in the land of 10,000 lakes, while Green Bay is a lot like Buffalo if you look outside Titletown and its identity surrounding the packers.
6th: Las Vegas, NV (Las Vegas Raiders, Week 6): 17/45
T-4th: Houston, TX (Houston Texans, Week 1) and Minneapolis, MN (Minnesota Vikings, Week 9/MNF): 27/45
3rd: Los Angeles, CA (Los Angeles Rams, Week 5/MNF): 30/45
2nd: Green Bay, WI (Green Bay Packers, Week 14/SNF): 32/45
1st: Denver, CO (Denver Broncos, Week 16/Christmas Day): 34/45
All said, the Bills' two non-divisional road games in December are the best to go to for fans for an overall good experience at the game and the surrounding things, so keep an eye out for plenty of blue and red and "Go Bills!" chants throughout the season.

title: Bills Criticized for the New Undersized Video Boards at Highmark Stadium
full_text:
The annual Return of the Blue & Red scrimmage took place on Saturday, but the practice wasn't the only major story this year.   While fans were thrilled to see the Buffalo Bills in action, the real focus was the brand new Highmark Stadium, which was debuted unofficially.
In a break from tradition, this event was reserved for season ticket holders . That led to some frustration for non-season ticket holders who planned to attend, but was also understandable considering the financial investment for personal seat licenses made by ticket holders.
Those who were able to gain access arrived early and soaked in all the highlights of the team's new home. Bills On SI writer Mike Moraitis summarized some of the best features , which include the Labatt Skyline Deck and extra leg room in the seats.
Not everything was positive, however. One criticism that was making the rounds on social media was the size of the video boards. Alex Brasky shared a clip from inside the stadium and called the size of the boards " underwhelming ." His video was shared by Yahoo! Sports , who asked fans for their opinion. A few fans said the video boards didn't matter, but more seemed to poke fun at the franchise for falling short of expectations.
The Bills opted for smaller video boards inside Highmark Stadium 🧐 What do you think of the decision? (🎥 @alexbrasky ) pic.twitter.com/O9vxrsNORM
I believe to have found what might well be the worst seat in the house. pic.twitter.com/2ywzoZplRT
The video board wasn't the only area that drew heat. Buffalo was also put on blast for seats with obstructed views. Images of those seats were also circulating on social media, showing seats that were blocked by stairs, video boards, and walkways.
Whoever designed the new Bills stadium should wasn't very keen to detail. Imagine paying tens of thousands on PSLs and season tickets and walk into a view like this... pic.twitter.com/mGhzbCaMVs
While it's not logical to expect every seat to have a perfect sightline, it does feel like an oversight to have seats with such obstruction in a brand new stadium. Another issue that was raised by fans was the significant climb to seats toward the top of the stadium, which some called steep while also pointing out there were no restrooms up high .
To be fair, the steep climb and lack of restrooms at the top of stadiums is not unique to Highmark. Instead, that's an unfortunate issue for fans at most stadiums.
A view from the absolute top of Highmark. A HIKE and a steep one at that. No bathrooms at the top - so you could be scaling this mountain multiple times a game. View is great but you gotta earn it. pic.twitter.com/bY192Reg9W
The Bills will have two games at home during the preseason , hosting the Carolina Panthers on August 15 and the Pittsburgh Steelers on the 27th. The regular season then begins on the road as they take on the Houston Texans in Week 1.
Their official home opener will take place in Week 2 , with the Detroit Lions visiting Buffalo on Thursday Night Football. All of the state-of-the-art features will be on display for that game, but according to the chatter on social media, there will be some fans left feeling disappointed by the experience.
In retrospect, it was not my intention to bring all the critics and pessimists out by posting one picture of one of the few bad seats at the Highmark. Of the 60,000-plus seats, people seem more into knocking the few bad ones. I consider the stadium to be very inviting.
